utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Welcome again to you all for 2006. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I just deal with one or two administrative matters to assist the Court? On the last occasion, just before Christmas, Your Honour asked us about disclosure and discovery. Can I just say that we did a second check on matters to be disclosed under Rule 68 and Rule 66 because clearly we had to rely on others before that date. We did find additional material which we have served on the Defence. It is both Rule 66 and Rule 68. It contains witnesses or statements of witnesses, some of whom have given evidence in the last term. It may be that it will require recalling of some of those witnesses but only in very shortened form and I know in conversation with my learned friends they would ask the Court until next Monday to clarify the extent of which they require any additional material. Secondly, in relation to the witness who gave evidence and is part heard, we have found another witness whose name I do not wish to mention in open court. My learned friends know. We would be seeking to call that witness, but that could only be done after the part-heard witness gives the evidence. And I see no difficulty in relation to that vis-a-vis the time scale. And then finally you asked about agreed facts. The facts have been agreed. Might I just indicate in relation to what I will call the Tomas Mercep evidence with the Defence -- are being -- asking questions of general nature about what was happening in May and June. Again, I've mentioned to my learned friends in a meeting with them that we do have confidential material about Mercep. We would not wish to disclose it. We have indicated the reasons in general terms why not and have said to them that if they wish to draft any agreed facts themselves or any facts they we propose we can agree I will look at them and try to do so. It will have the benefit of not creating difficulties administratively and may well move the Court through at a greater speed. So in relation to all matters administrative matters, I think are in hand, and that my learned friends will make applications as they deem appropriate. Finally, on a personal note, I wonder if I could make application for reasons that I have given and do not wish to rehearse in open court, whether in actual fact the court could not sit, or would not mind sitting on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Moore. I take it you have discussed the motion about Friday with Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: They are privy to all the matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the Chamber not sitting on Friday to accommodate Mr. Moore's situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic [sic]. The Chamber indicates that it will not sit on Friday of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic to his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to say something about what my colleague has just raised before the Chamber. I'm talking about the multitude of documents that were served on the Defence teams by the OTP between mid-December and today. We have made a promise to the Trial Chamber. We have lived up to this promise. We have used the recess period to good effect and we have managed to deal with all the outstanding issues that we were not able to deal with due to late disclosure at the beginning of this trial. The Defence has been successful in this task. Then we found ourselves facing this situation in which the OTP served on us about 4.500 pages of documents pursuant to both 66(A)(ii) and Rule 68. What causes particular concern to the Defence is that out of the 14 witnesses heard, we received statements in relation to eight of those pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii). The Defence finds this sort of practice to be of concern. Over the long term this might affect the preparation of our Defence and our strategy of cross-examination. The Defence remains adamant that the witnesses called by the OTP -- that their appearance be accompanied by the relevant statements. On the one hand, bearing in mind the interests of our clients and the duties and obligations of the Defence under the Statute, and on the other hand in order to expedite proceedings, which is a process that the Defence should actively be contributing to, the Defence teams would like to have until Monday to announce our position on which witnesses we believe should be recalled, and on which particular aspects of their testimony the witnesses will be re-examined by the Defence. The Defence wishes to use this time in order to examine all the circumstances involved. We want to give our clients what they are due on the one hand, and not further burden the proceedings. However, it seems that this manner of disclosing documents is something that we can expect to continue in the future. Our colleagues have informed us that this is due so certain problems that the OTP have encountered in their work at an earlier date. However, the Defence believes that regardless of what the causes may be for this situation to have come about, this practice in general is prejudicial to the Defence. Therefore I would like to ask if my colleague could inform the Defence teams since when the OTP have been in possession of these documents pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii), in relation to the witnesses that have already been heard or part heard so as to avoid this practice from being applied in the future. As for these concerns relating to the documents that we have received, my colleague will probably speak more about that and I will not go any further into the matter now. I do wish to raise two other matters before the Chamber nonetheless. One, in relation to the witness who was part heard, and who still needs to be cross-examined by Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence. In view of the fact that we received a new statement in relation to this witness, would it be possible for the other Defence teams to be given a chance to re-examine the witness? We believe this would be a just and equitable course of action. Secondly, as one of the results of our work throughout this period of time, the Defence has been able to do what we have promised to the Trial Chamber. We tracked down Mr. Raseta and asked him about the challenged signature on MFI 40, the document that was marked for identification. I'm now able to say that he has confirmed the authenticity of that particular signature. We no longer challenge the fact that he indeed signed that document and we may deal with this matter in due course if necessary. Thank you very much, Your Honours. That's all I have to say for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. Vasic, and I apologise that I looked at the wrong end of the bar table. To the extent that you propose to -- or ask whether you might have leave to further cross-examine, if the additional statement or statements that have been made available to you open up some new area or introduce some new element you certainly may. So don't worry about that, and I would no doubt expect that both you and Mr. Moore would be able to reach agreement as to whether there was justification in what has now been served to -- for you to have a further opportunity to cross-examine. Are you wanting now, Mr. Lukic, to have your say? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have made this clear enough. My greetings to you, Your Honours and to all the participants in these proceedings. I will try not to repeat myself but I do wish to say a couple of words about this issue which I believe is crucial to the Defence's position on those witnesses who have already testified. On cross-examination, we were greatly gladdened by the Chamber's approach on cross-examination in general. You've always given us an opportunity to organise ourselves without taking unnecessary breaks. This has been very effective practice so far. The fact that we have now been given new statements in relation to witnesses who have already testified does cause us a great deal of prejudice and we wish to place this on the transcript. The fact that these witnesses may appear again, the fact that we may be given a chance to cross-examine them on certain portions of their testimony, which proved inconsistent, and that is what seems to be the case here, as far as we can tell, is prejudicial to what we have so far been able to establish through our cross-examination of these witnesses. This is what causes the Defence concern. If a certain amount of damage has already been done, and there is nothing can be done about that, may the Trial Chamber please try to exert influence on the OTP that such practice is not repeated and does not continue in the future. You know that when you go back to an old subject, your cross-examination is no longer as effective as it may have been originally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One thing I have to underline, though --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sometimes it's been my experience that that is correct. Sometimes you get a new opening. There is no universal experience about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sure you have much more experience in this matter than we do. I'm just considering our position, the position that we were in at the time, when these witnesses were being heard; I do agree with you that there is no general rule about this, however. What we have been talking about is not in relation to this particular OTP team but to the OTP in general. This is the third time that the Defence has been prejudiced to some extent in its work. You will remember that we were granted extra time in preparation to this trial precisely because of the multitude of documents that we have been given. You will also remember that sometimes we were given addenda to witness's testimonies 20 minutes [as interpreted] before they actually entered the courtroom. This has improved and addenda have been arriving in a more timely manner. Notes were taken at the 65 ter Conference in February 2004, you might as well wish to go back to those notes. We asked that the OTP give us all the documents they had at the time and their reaction was they did not wish to cover us in documents. That was at the pre-trial stage which would have been a suitable moment for us to start these preparations. I do not wish to complain but I do wish to have these concerns recorded on the transcript. There is an error in the transcript. I said 24 hours on page 7, line 12. In order to make a joint effort to expedite these proceedings, in order to keep the trial running, as it were, and in order not to cause any impediments to the smooth running of this trial, by next Monday we will be informing the Chamber about our position, that is whether we wish to have any of the witnesses recalled. The final decision will be down to you, Your Honours, needless to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Moore, the position has been put that a very large number of documents have been discovered for the first time over the break. Could you assist the Chamber with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. The situation is that this case, as the Court knows, was earmarked, there was an application for it to go 11 bis to another jurisdiction. There was material in OTP existing at that time, that's material that's now been served. A decision was taken not by this team that as it was going to go as they thought by way of 11 bis to another jurisdiction, that that material would then not be served. And when the Court reminded us -- indeed, we have been doing it any way we have been double checking as much as we possibly can, this case, because of its nature, goes into many areas and we located on a second search in December a block of material that should have been disclosed and had not been disclosed. And I have apologised to my learned friends on behalf of the OTP. It does not assist to say -- well thankfully we did find it. But it had been discovered and it should have been disclosed actually probably in April or May of last year because it was available then. But a decision was taken to not withhold it in any malicious way but as it were to forward it to the jurisdiction and let the counsel who was involved then deal with the problem. That seems to be the rationale and I've spoken to the senior trial attorney and indeed the case manager or had the case manager spoken to, to find out why it was this material was not to the forefront of disclosure as early as possible, and I'm not going to try and excuse something that clearly should have been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When was this served, this material?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We discovered it in -- I believe it was discovered in December, early part of December and it was served before Christmas and after Christmas. It's not a basically a tranche of material. One thing has led to another and we have, as it were, followed routes and served it as soon as we have found it, but material -- I was in Belgrade up until the 22nd, 23rd and I was in contact with Mr. Lukic then to inform him that there was material that clearly should have been disclosed and had not been disclosed by an earlier team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean that to be December or January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was certainly in correspondence and speaking to Mr. Lukic then. May I just clarify? Would Your Honour forgive me for a moment? No, the dates that I've said are correct. So certainly notice was given and some material was given, a large amount of it, was given before what I would call our Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, is it the case that you have now discovered and disclosed -- sorry, have you now disclosed all the material of which you're aware?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't believe there is any other material apart from what I will call the Mercep material and there clearly is material on Mercep. I don't want to go into any discussions in open court in relation to it. What I've said to my learned friends is rather than have perhaps what I will call full blown legal arguments about the admissibility or otherwise of it, if in actual fact the Defence wish to place before the Prosecution a series of what I will call prospective admissions or agreed facts, I will see whether in actual fact I am able to agree those facts, and if I can agree the facts, then it does not require cross-examination by them. There is nothing there that I can see in the material that I have that necessarily would be exculpatory or indeed I would even question the relevance of the material but the topic has been raised and therefore I've got to deal with it. But one of ways in my jurisdiction of dealing with a problem that may be contentious is to say to the Defence, or the Prosecution, if you give me a set of propositions I may be able to agree that and that will satisfy all parties. So I'm certainly willing to consider that option. If that is not available, then clearly we will have to come before the Court in an ex parte application and I give the Defence notice it will be an application, ex parte, but not on the topic as such although it's obvious what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Leaving aside the Mercep component, you are able now to indicate that there has been disclosure of all known, relevant material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To this stage we have disclosed all known, relevant material but I say quite honestly because of this situation, we have decided to look at everything again from other teams and before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that, Mr. Moore. I think in the situation, nothing more is called for by way of decision or order on the part of the Chamber at this moment. Clearly, we will allow the Defence until Monday, as they have indicated, to indicate whether witnesses are needed to be recalled. If there is any difficulty about those, that will be dealt with when those indications are given. At the moment, there is no backlog, as it were, of material to be discovered that is known to Mr. Moore so I think we can leave all that situation as it is. So, Mr. Moore, are we ready to move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My learned friend Ms. Tuma will deal with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please take the affirmation card and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like the witness to state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Aernaut van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what are your profession today?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I am currently employed as a Professor at the American university in Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And I would like the witness, Mr. Van Lynden, to give us an outline of your professional background?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I began as a journalist at the beginning of 1979 working for a Dutch newspaper, the Haagsche Courant, the newspaper of The Hague, covering the Middle East and southern Europe. In September 1980 I was in Baghdad when Saddam Hussein launched the war on Iran. I covered that conflict from both sides in 1980. At the beginning of 1981 I became a freelance journalist working under contract for BBC radio, the Washington Post newspaper, and the Observer newspaper in Britain, and with my base as buy route, covered the wars, the various wars in Lebanon, the Iran-Iraq conflict and the Soviet occupation in Afghanistan. In 1986 I left Beirut and moved to London. There I worked for a year for Granada television, and then in 1988 joined Sky Television, helped set up Sky News, a 24-hour news channel, and worked for Sky News until 2001, covering basically the various crises in Eastern Europe in 1989, including the Romanian revolution in December 1989, the Gulf War of 1990 and 1991, from 1991 in the summer, June 1991 onwards, I covered the various conflicts of Yugoslavia's disintegration.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Van Lynden. And when you were working as a journalist and covering as I understand it different wars, in what kind of capacity, what kind of specialty did you have as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was, I suppose, always a political-military journalist and I would be classed, I suppose, as a war correspondent.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And may I ask you when did you actually start to work and to cover different wars as a war correspondent?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The first war I covered was the war in Lebanon and I first went to Lebanon in 1979. So right at the beginning of my journalistic career I began covering armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what kind of conflicts that you had been able to observe and to report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: -- during your profession as a war correspondent?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I covered a variety of conflicts, both conflicts between nations so between armies, for instance the war between Iran and Iraq, and conflicts within one society, for instance the conflict in Lebanon where there were different militias, often very many different militias, for instance the Palestinians were divided in all sorts of groupings within Lebanon, as were the Christian forces, as were the Muslim forces. There were armies operating there as well, the Israeli army, the Syrian army, but it was a quite different conflict than that in which two nation states are embroiled in a war between each other as the Iran Iraq war or as the war that took place for the liberation of Kuwait in 1991 when you had the organised armed forces of a country fighting each other. For us as journalists, it's generally more easy to operate within the sort of anarchy that exists within a civil conflict as, for instance in Lebanon. When one is dealing with the armed forces, the organised armed forces of a single nation-state, then usually those armed forces are better organised and will also try to keep tighter control of journalists like myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Van Lynden. When you were reporting, as you tell us now, from different kinds of wars, what is your experience from that period of time? Were you out in the war itself and observed it? So you were in the middle of it? Or did you observe it from a distance?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As a war correspondent one does different things. One is not always on the front lines but one of the things that one absolutely tries to do is to observe it firsthand how the military forces of any side are behaving. Now obviously in a war between two countries, for instance the Iran Iraq war, it is not possible to cross lines. You are either with the forces of one side or the other. Nor was it possible for instance in 1991 during the war in Croatia for me to cross lines. That was possible during the subsequent war in Bosnia in 1992 to 1995. But you go to the front lines you look at what kind of armaments are used, you look at what type of organisation the various units have, how good the command and control is, how good the tactical and strategic behaviour the armed forces that you are with, you look at various aspects. But it is not limited to that. You also, of course, look at wider things as the effects on a society, propaganda, what the governments are doing, what negotiations are taking place. It's a variety of things that is included but certainly, one of the chief things is for us to go to the front lines or as close as we can get to observe the soldiers and the officers in the war that is taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you if you do have any kind of military background and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I as a Dutch man had to do military service which still existed in the 1970s in the Netherlands and I served in the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps, a small and on the whole professional unit, but they did take small groups once a year of reservists for reserve officer training. It's a one-year training to become a second Lieutenant and then one had to serve for at the minimum of at least another year as a second Lieutenant, and I served for about two and a half years with the marine corps before I became a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When was this in time?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: From the summer of 1976 until the end of 1978.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Van Lynden, you just mentioned that you covered the war in former Yugoslavia. And can you give us an outline and describe for us where you did, if and you did have an office, from which you operated from and how that office was set up?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was first sent to Yugoslavia in June 1991 when I was sent to Slovenia, to the Slovenian capital Ljubljana on the day the Slovenes declared their independence from the rest of the Yugoslav federation. After being in Slovenia for around two weeks, I was withdrawn from there and sent to Belgrade to cover the further events that took place from Belgrade and really from mid-July or the second half of July 1999 -- 1991 onwards, I was based in Belgrade and covered the entire conflict between the Serbs and the Croats from the Serb side, with my base being in Belgrade. In Belgrade, Sky News had contact with a man then working for Belgrade television, Jaksa Cekic [phoen], and he helped to set up an initial office within Belgrade television. He found a freelance Yugoslav, not a Serb, but a Yugoslav, to work with me as my field producer and interpreter. Initially, when working, we -- in July 1991, we worked with the crews of Belgrade television that happened to be in the field. From the beginning of August 1991 onwards Sky News sent a -- camera crews and editor so that's a three-man team a camera man a sound recordist and a pick fur editor from London and we continued to work like that. The freelance field producer that had been found by Jaksa in July 1991 continued to work with me throughout the conflict in Yugoslavia until 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. When you were out on mission in the former Yugoslavia and you did have your office based in Belgrade and then I understand that you were a team that worked and were out in the field to cover events that occurred. You mentioned three people in that team but was it so normally or could that change?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No the basic team for a television news reporting team that goes into the field consists of a correspondent, a field producer, a cameraman, and a sound recordist. So four people.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. In addition to the Belgrade office, did you have any other office set up in the neighbourhood or --

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Sky News deployed a separate team in Zagreb to cover the conflict from the Croatian side in 1991. Later during the war in Bosnia we had various teams located in various places depending on what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When it comes to your mission, if I may say so, in Croatia, it was the base in Belgrade that you worked from?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: With your team?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And when did you now arrive in Croatia for the first time?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In July -- shortly -- in fact almost immediately after I arriving in Belgrade we set off the day after my arrival in Belgrade, I set off with the field producer. We drove to a town in Bosnia called Bihac and initially based ourselves there, and then we went into Banija, the Banija region, a town called Dvor Na Uni, and there encountered Serb militia, a man called Captain Dragan, who took us with him on the day that he took the town of Glina. We remained in that area for several days, finally drove down to Knin in the Krajina, a separate area within Croatia, stayed there for several days, met again with Captain Dragan and also with a man who appeared to be in control there called Milan Martic. At a certain moment we were withdrawn back to Belgrade because the troika of the European Union, which I think at that time still was called the European Community, arrived for negotiations with the leadership in Belgrade and we returned to Belgrade to cover those talks and it was at that moment that a crew and an editor were sent out to help me from London, and that we no longer worked with Serbian cameramen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay so from that point of view from that time you were working only with your own cameraman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. And when did you enter the Eastern Slavonia part the first time?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, the first time we went in was in September 1991. Possibly late August.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And why did you?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The conflict was spreading. The conflict had initially started in Knin, in the Krajina, but by that stage fighting had also broken out in Eastern Slavonia, and so we went there to see to look at that conflict and see what we could find. Initially, we crossed into Eastern Slavonia at the bridge at Erdut and were taken to a variety of locations, including at a certain moment to Brsadin which is -- lies west, this is the northern front, north of Vukovar and Borovo Naselje, but Brsadin lies to the west of the town and this was a significant place because the Serbs had taken a grain silo there which in a countryside that is as flat as Eastern Slavonia therefore provides the high ground, so to speak, high ground specifically for military observers. And we were taken into the silo. We saw the observers at work, and it gave us a higher view as well as to the war happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You're saying here that you were taken into. You were taken. Who did take you? Was there any kind of -- did -- could you go on your own initiative or was it any body who did give you permission or can you tell us more about that? What do you mean by you were taken into your different locations?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Firstly it's a one of the basics of being a war correspondent that while one takes risks, one calculates the risks. If one is as one almost invariably is in someone else's country, one has to take care and simply driving in without knowing what the precise situation on the ground is is foolhardy to say the least. But apart from that, one needed permissions to cross either -- cross the bridge at Erdut into Eastern Slavonia, or along the road from Sid to Tovarnik, and that leads on to Oriolik, Negoslavci, and Vukovar, and the permissions we needed were from the federal Ministry of the Defence in Belgrade. We would need to get a piece of paper and a permission from them to be able to cross through the checkpoints into Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: May I ask you, did you receive a general permission or was it separate permissions? Can you tell us more about how it was done practically?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I remember it, we needed permission for every single day. This entailed that right at the beginning I went with my field producer Zoran Kusavac [phoen] to the ministry to their spokesman's office or their press office, I can't remember precisely what they called it, and we had meetings there explaining what we wanted to do. It was then explained to us that we would need these permissions and that they would did have to be given basically on a daily basis. After that it meant that Mr. Kusavac would usually go to the ministry in the late afternoon or evening to get a permission for the next day. When we started going in via Sid and Tovarnik, this was the main road where you do not cross the Danube, this is the highway from Serbia to Croatia, the army had opened a separate press office in the town of Sid. That's still on the Serb side of the border. And we would have to go to that office as well to get a subsequent permission to be able to drive on into Eastern Slavonia proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: These permissions, were there any conditions attached to those permissions?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not that I remember but we didn't always get them. So we were given them on some days but not on other days.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Was there any reason given for that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When you didn't get the permissions?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Was it always the Ministry of Defence that you approached in order to have the permission?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And were you guaranteed to have access to the routes even with the permission?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Access to the ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: For the different locations that you were visiting, when you did -- when you did have a permission, was that a guarantee for you to be able to enter whatever location you were aiming at?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. We would -- it depended on the units that one encountered once one got there. We'd be given permission to cross over. For instance, I remember at a certain moment, I think this is in October 1991, that we crossed from Sid to Tovarnik, drove up the road to Oriolik and there were checkpoints on the way, military checkpoints on the way. They let us through. At Oriolik one would have to basically turn right towards the village of Negoslavci. We had had an interview that day with a general from the JNA who had said we would be allowed to enter Vukovar itself. In Negoslavci we were stopped and there, as I recall, a, what I think we would refer to as a political commissar, stopped us and said that we would not be allowed to go any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: M'hm. I would like you, Mr. Van Lynden, to look at a map and for the Court officer, it is Exhibit 103. It will soon appear on the screen on your left side. In the compilation, the map is also available for the Court. Okay. Mr. Van Lynden, do you have the map on?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah. You recognise the area here I guess, of course --

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: -- having been there a lot. Can you please on this map show us what route you were normally -- okay. We'll see. You normally did take when you were travelling in this area? You mentioned that you had your office based in Belgrade and that you -- for every separate journey you have to have a permission in order to enter the territory of, let us say, Croatia, at the time, and please show us on this map what route you did normally take on those commissions?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The main road that I was referring to that it's -- the highway is what I'm drawing now. It leads past Sid and this is a motor way until Sid, and there, if this is the road that we took most often, this would then lead to Tovarnik and from Tovarnik on to Oriolik and then at Oriolik we could go up to Negoslavci, and then from Negoslavci we were towards the end of the conflict for -- the end of the battle of Vukovar allowed to go -- continue to go on into Vukovar itself. The other road is north of there, the crossing is at Erdut. This is a bridge across the River Danube. And there, the road, how we precisely got there, I -- I cannot remember. As far as I'm aware we crossed at Erdut two or three times and many more times at the south but the road to Erdut is a different road than the road to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When you did go to via Erdut, so to say, did -- then you went or came also from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was always from Belgrade so it was always, well, from the right-hand side of the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. And can you just briefly tell us, in general terms, under -- during what period in time you were taking those routes? Normally you took the route, as you said here, Tovarnik-Oriolik up to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Was it -- which kind of period did you travel?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is September and October. I then left for a period. I was sent home for a break, and I returned in November and the first trip I made back there was on the 12th of November and that's when we were able to enter Vukovar directly, and in fact spend a night in Vukovar. The initial trip that I took up this road from Sid to Tovarnik we only got as far as the village of Ilaca, which is before Oriolik. Yes you see it on the map here, Ilaca just the name is just above Tovarnik. There the houses in the village were still burning when we were taken up there and the last part of that journey we did not do in our own soft skin cars but we were put in a -- into an armoured personnel carrier of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to describe during those occasions when you were travelling this route, as you just mentioned, what kind of observations did you do in terms of destructions of villages, for instance. Tell us what you saw during -- when you were driving through that route.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The first time that we entered Tovarnik, I believe Tovarnik had actually fallen to the JNA a week beforehand. There was significant destruction there. In Tovarnik there was both a Catholic and an Orthodox church. Both of them were severely damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Please talk a bit slower, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: And there was significant damage to the houses in the village. There were some civilians there but these were only Serbs. There were no longer any Croat civilians, we were told in the village. It was on that occasion that we were then taken on further to the village of Ilaca. And there, as I already said, houses were still actually burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, when you're talking about significant damage, would you more describe that, make a picture for us, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That would mean that there was not -- the houses in this part of Eastern Slavonia, in the villages, don't have a normal front door in the sense that we have them in the streets of The Hague, for instance. The doors are usually within courtyards. There are windows along the street but rather sort of gates to a courtyard before one enters the house and what you would see is that every single house was pockmarked by bullets. Some houses had also been hit by heavier weaponry, whether tanks or antitank rockets, something of that nature. Certain houses were almost completely destroyed. In Tovarnik, I don't remember buildings still burning but some, there was still smoke rising from them. For instance the Catholic church there. In Ilaca there were house that is were completely destroyed and still on fire. And so there was -- I don't remember seeing any house that had not been touched by gunfire of one short sort or another. Some had been hit much harder than others and some were completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. And you were travelling in this area for quite some time, as you told us now. Can you tell us if there was an escalation in the damage or if it was the same the whole time of the villages?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't remember there being worse damage to Tovarnik or Ilaca after these had fallen into the hands of the JNA but as I said the destruction was pretty pronounced in -- and certainly in Ilaca, as I said, whole houses were burning. The same is true after we -- when we first Oriolik, Negoslavci. There was some damage. It did not seem to become worse after they had fallen into the hands of the JNA, no. But there was significant damage done in capturing these villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When you were travelling in -- I'm referring to that route that we have been talking about, were there any checkpoints on the way?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were checkpoints. There was a checkpoint on what would have been the official border between Serbia and Croatia, and there were checkpoints in villages where you could be stopped and your papers checked. In between the villages, there were no checkpoints, and the road between Tovarnik and Oriolik became -- was always a dangerous road to take because there are corn fields along the side and throughout the conflict in Vukovar, these were not cleared by the JNA and they were at times used by Croatian snipers who would take a small ladder with them, set that up in the corn field, which provided very good cover, take one shot at a passing car, and then disappear again. We were shot at on a number of occasions and the Yugoslav army soldiers that we encountered also complained that this happened to them throughout those months of the fighting around Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Before I move on here I would like to -- the court officers to tender the map, the marked map, into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit number 134, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When you were travelling in this area, that is before you entering, as you said earlier, Vukovar on the 12th November, what observations did you do in terms of army around in this area? What army it was, what kind of equipment this army had at the time, and if there was more than one army, for instance, paramilitary units, so please describe that for us and that -- in this area that you were describing earlier.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Between Tovarnik, Oriolik, Negoslavci and then in Vukovar, what we encountered was full units of the Yugoslav army, territorials, and later on, but this is only later on, in this -- on this side, that we encountered units of men who would describe themselves either as what they themselves called, they said that they were Chetniks, a word that we were loathe to use because of its connotation back to the Second World War or more usually they would describe themselves as being militiamen of Mr. Seselj. On the northern side, from Erdut, at Erdut, we encountered a quite separate militia led by a man called Zeljko Raznjatovic, otherwise known as Arkan, whom I met on various occasions, and who on two occasions took us to his barracks, training ground, which was close to Erdut, and there we saw his men and talked to him. I never saw him or his men in action, but we did see them there. But that was a quite separate unit. At that time, as I recall, they did not call themselves the Tigers, as they did later during the war in Bosnia, and they were allied to a man who described himself as the political leader of the Serbs in Eastern Slavonia, a man called Goran Hadzic, whom we also met.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Will you describe the equipment?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The equipment that we saw was of a variety, I mean the soldiers had their infantry weapon, basically the Kalashnikov rifle. We -- Arkan's men were -- had different weaponry, usually western, often Heckler and Koch submachine-guns, some with silencers on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We saw armoured personnel carriers, nearly all mounted with heavy machine-guns. We saw a variety of tanks, both old and new, and with the old even going as far back as the T-33 which is of second year -- Second World War vintage but also the more modern one created in Yugoslavia, the M-84. We saw heavy artillery of various calibres, multiple rocket-launchers, mostly of 128 millimetre. We saw heavy mortars, 120-millimetre mortars, and I saw the light mortar, the 60-millimetre mortar. The full range of weaponry of a fall army. The artillery was always deployed in batteries and we were taken to them on several occasions and allowed to film them, also when they were firing. Mortar units of 120-millimetre, again, deployed as standard mortar units, and I was myself trained as a mortarist in the Dutch marine corps so I have direct knowledge of that. And then yes, well all the -- all the weaponry including anti-aircraft guns which I never saw fired there on the ground in the sense that they were used as simply machine-guns. But I was told that they had been used in that way, that they were for instance during the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you see anything from the Croatian side, in terms of equipment?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The only time I directly saw the Croatian fighters was either those that had been killed already in combat or those that surrendered on the 18th of November, who came out of Mitnica, the Mitnica district of Vukovar, who handed who literally laid their guns on the ground. These were Kalashnikovs, pistols, revolvers, all light weaponry. I didn't see any heavy weaponry. I suspect the Croats must have had mortars, they will have had some anti-tank rockets. We could certainly tell that they had antitank mines and lighter mines, but as far as I'm aware, they did not have tanks or heavy artillery or armoured personnel carriers at their disposal apart from possibly one or two police armoured vehicles that they may have had. But I never saw any of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Also referring back to when you were travelling in this area and you give description of what kind of weaponry was used, what -- how was the shelling? Was it a two-way shelling or can you describe anything about that when you were travelling in this area more or less every day?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I only saw outgoing fire. I never experienced incoming fire on to the JNA lines from the Croatian side. I only saw fire of various calibres as I've described going out from JNA positions. Both heavy artillery fire and tank fire and heavy mortar fire and light mortar fire. While I'm aware that at certain moments we did come under fire ourselves being with the JNA this only came from rifle fire. Never from heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You were, Mr. Van Lynden, you were in the area and can you also describe in the way of how intensive this single way of shelling was?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, it depended on what day you went there. This was a period of a -- large numbers of cease-fires which were declared in Belgrade by the various mediators that were brought in to try and mediate a peaceful end to this conflict. And we would go there on days expecting that there be no fire and then yet suddenly there was. I remember one particular day in October 1991, that again we met this general, who I think was a Major General in the Yugoslav army and a convoy was meant to enter Vukovar to bring food, medicine, into Vukovar and take out the wounded from Vukovar. He assured us that this was happening and that there was a complete cease-fire and that we would get access to the route that this convoy would take. We then drove up to Negoslavci. There we were stopped. There a lower-ranking officer, I think a Major or a Lieutenant Colonel, said to us that this convoy was not going to be entering, that there was no cease-fire. We then saw ambulances ferrying wounded from Vukovar to Negoslavci from where they were taken out by helicopters to the hospitals in Belgrade and heavy fire from the artillery batteries around Negoslavci. We were not allowed to enter Vukovar that day but there was clearly no cease-fire. There was heavy fighting going on. Who started that fire, of course, I cannot say. As far as I recall, both sides accused the other of breaking the cease-fire agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: This was in October and --

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Also, during that observation time that you did have from September until November 1991 in this area, you described the army and the sort of differences between the JNA and the Croats. You have described destructions. How about civilians? Did you see any civilians in this area? Did you see any column of civilians, refugees?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing refugees. I do remember that there were, when we first entered Tovarnik, for instance, that there were civilians there. As I recall, the Orthodox bishop actually was visiting Tovarnik and we spoke to him. But he did not live in Tovarnik. But he was having a look at the destruction and he in fact explained to us that in his opinion it was impossible for Croats and Serbs to live together, which we found a slightly strange statement for a man of the cloth to make. But there were certainly civilians still in Tovarnik. I do not remember seeing any civilians in Ilaca why where the destruction was heavier even than Tovarnik and where as I have earlier said the houses were still burning. It was only later on in Vukovar itself that we did encounter civilians. This is on the morning of the 13th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: We will arrive to that later, please?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Also during this time frame from September to November 1991 when you were travelling in this area, were you able to film, to do -- to make films during the -- of your observations?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we were able to film but we were not always able to get to the places where we wanted to get to film. Filming was often difficult. We -- the usually -- the rule became within the team when we went out there that we would be lucky to film anything before 1.00 in the afternoon. We would leave Belgrade usually at 4 or 4.30 in the morning. By the time we had received the second permission in Sid and then continued on and had got through all the roadblocks, it could often be the afternoon before we had come anywhere close to the front lines. And there were days that we weren't allowed for reasons that were unspecified to go any further and therefore there were days of frustration for us that we weren't really able to film what was happening. I remember one day that it was raining, there was shooting going on, we were able to film multiple rocket launcher site that was firing but we were not allowed to go further. It was not explained to us why. So we could film with the unit that we had reached but we were not allowed to go any further and film the actual front line fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You said that you were not allowed to go any further. Who did not allow you that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was usually at a checkpoint that would be stopped, and there would be some officer standing there. And there were occasions as I said that even when we had had permission from a Major general that further down the road you can encounter a lower officer of the rank of major or Lieutenant Colonel, at times I think people it would acted as political commissars, who would not allow us to go further. I think I need to add one thing here, that the Yugoslav professional officers had been indoctrinated to believe that all Westerners were suspect but that all western journalists were almost by definition spies. And so they distrusted our presence and often made it very difficult for us to do our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Were there any kind of censorship when it comes to -- for your ability to film?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There was no censorship in the direct sort that anyone from the Yugoslav authorities would check our tapes or check my script before it was sent to London. The censorship happened in a different means in that they wouldn't always allow us to go through to the front lines and film everything that we would have wanted to on any specific day. There wasn't free access in that sense. But I was never censored as I, for instance, was under the censorship laws in 1991 with the American forces in the Gulf War, where an officer would check both what we had filmed and the script that I had written. This did not occur. The censorship occurred in a different sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were making observations. And how did you then report it? You have just described for us that you were travelling in this area under specific time frame and you have your location base in Belgrade. How was it done when you -- how did you report back out to the world that you were the Sky News in London?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There was still the technological difficulties that existed at that time and no mobile phones yet, no immediate satellite telephones available that are available today. And therefore what we needed to do on each occasion if we wanted to file a report we would have to go back to Belgrade, edit the story there, and send it by satellite from Belgrade television. That was our basic way of reporting the war. If I wanted and felt that it was important to try to send any kind of report by telephone, I would again have to leave Eastern Slavonia, get back into Serbia, then try to find a telephone and get a connection to London, which was not that simple. But basically what we did is leave Belgrade early in the morning and return in the late afternoon to then file a report and send it to London and then go the next morning again.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Were there any deadlines in the afternoon or late afternoon or in the evening for you to file a report back to London?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, I worked for Sky News which is a 24-hour news channel and has a deadline every single hour. One of the problems of modern journalism, I would contend. There was always a hope from the offers that we would certainly get reports back for the six or 7.00 bulletin in London. With a time difference that meant we had one hour more in Belgrade. But a story to edit takes nearly -- at least an hour to do so we would always try to be back by five, six, 7.00 at the very latest.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Van Lynden, you mentioned here that you were in a specific training camp, at least on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: At Erdut yes, near to Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what you observed in that training camp and who were there who were active, what it looked like, how many people were in that camp? Can you please describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is the training camp run by Mr. Raznjatovic whom I mentioned earlier. Better known under the name Arkan. There were a number of huts, as far as I can recall. He had an office there, spoke to us there, introduced us to a number of other commanders under him, and we met around 50 or 60 of his men. They were not dressed in Yugoslav uniforms. They were generally wearing western combat camouflage gear, different kinds of boots, and western boots rather than those of the Yugoslav army. And I recall there weaponry was quite different. We are dealing here with western weaponry. Some heavy, I mean heavy machine-guns and antitank rocket propellants, or weapons like the Heckler and Koch submachine-gun which is German made, the Yugoslav army, as far as I'm aware did not have.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We will move on to -- I would like to move on to Vukovar. When was the first time when you entered Vukovar with your team?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I cannot remember the precise date but we were told by the army that they had secured the JNA barracks on the southern side of Vukovar, on the southern edge of Vukovar, and we were taken to those barracks in an armoured personnel carrier of the Yugoslav army. There were still fighting going on. We could hear the fighting. The fighting that we heard was of rifle fire and we were taken in, and we ran out of the armoured personnel carrier into a command and control room a wireless office within the JNA barracks, and as far as I remember, this was in October 1991 but I do not recall the precise date. We didn't stay there very long, for half an hour maybe. And we were then driven out in the same way that we came in, in the armoured personnel carrier back. As far as I can recall we left our own cars at Negoslavci and were driven the last part in the armoured personnel carriers of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Can you describe the JNA barracks at that time? It was October 1991, if I recall it -- you correctly.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Can I -- my recollection, we were sitting inside the armoured personnel carrier and then were rushed inside in, into a room, so I haven't got a very precise picture in my head of what the entire JNA barracks looked like. But as far as I recall, the roofs were still standing, they were not burned down. The various barracks there were -- still seemed to be in good condition, and the office is -- that we entered, this command and control and where the wirelesses were, seemed to be in good condition. Not as if anything had happened to them or that they had been trashed by anyone. So that the -- basically the condition of the barracks seemed as far as I could see from within the armoured personnel carrier and while I was there, in good condition.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. And the next -- next occasion when you entered into Vukovar, when was that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That was on the 12th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: By what means, do you remember that date, the 12th of November? How can you say it was the 12th November?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I remember it very clearly because it was a day unlike other days that I had in 1991 in Yugoslavia, because on that date, we actually drove ourselves into Vukovar and I had been away for 10 days or two weeks, and this was my first day working back in -- in the country and there we were -- we met up with an officer whom my field producer had met earlier in that month, and who allowed us, gave us contact with to a good army unit, a guard unit, and we actually stayed with that unit for more than 24 hours, stayed the night with them on front lines, and only returned to Belgrade the following day. And this was a quite separate experience to the other experiences and that's why it sticks very clearly in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. You say that you did have -- get access you stayed with a guard unit. Of which army was that guard unit?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was of the Yugoslav army, a guard unit, a professional unit of the Yugoslav army, dressed in a different manner than the normal Yugoslav soldiers, different clothes, different helmets, absolute professional unit, different bearing, both of the soldiers of the non-commissioned officers and of the officers, a unit of professional soldiers who had been clearly well trained.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Were you allowed to be with your team together with that guard unit for 24 hour?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. And so they did follow you or were they taking you to different locations or can you describe what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. As I recall, we drove into -- it may have been into the JNA barracks on the south of town, where my field producer said that he had met a more senior officer within the guards of the JNA. This was a man who's present here, Mr. Sljivancanin, whom my field producer had already met. He introduced me. He told me then that he had had contact with another British journalist from channel 4 news, and we asked for his permission and for him if he could organise to put us in touch with a unit that fell under him, and we were taken to a, as I recall, a Lieutenant - I'm not sure whether he was is an a second or a first Lieutenant - of a platoon commander and we stayed then with that platoon for the next 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, you mentioned here his permission, who is permission are you --

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Sljivancanin's permission.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When you met Mr. Sljivancanin, how did he act in that you did have some -- you did have a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, a man who was in command. We had a perfectly proper conversation. We asked him, we explained what we wanted to do, that we wanted to be with the front line unit. He was in agreement that that should be possible. I also made clear that I wished very much to be with a professional unit. Again this comes back to the same reasoning that I told the Court earlier, that in a war zone you take risks, but you try to calculate the risks and I feel happier being with what I consider to be a professional unit rather than being with a militia unit or with a unit of the reserves and these were professional men. He accepted that and said that he would arrange it, and arrange it he did. He himself appeared as a professional officer and as a man who was in command and used to giving orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When you were did spent time with this unit were you able to talk to the soldiers in the unit?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we were, both during the day and then, of course, in the evening and during the night. I don't recall us sleeping a lot. We were told that we were sleeping about 50 or 60 metres from the Croat lines so it was very much a front-line position in a house, just in a normal civilian house that had been taken over by the soldiers. Yes, we were able to speak both to the Lieutenant and to his commander, a man with the rank of Captain, whom I recall being called Mladen Maric to the sergeants and to the men. And we had various conversations. I do have to say to the court though that those conversations went via my field producer. I do not speak Serbo-Croat and therefore the field producer was translating the conversations that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what kind of information did you get? What was the content of those conversations? Can you give us an example of that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Different. I mean firstly we asked about the nature of the war that they were fighting and they explained that it was a war for house to house, street to street, almost that every house, every street, was a separate battle. They also explained to us that it was extremely dangerous and that one of their men had been wounded that day either by stepping on a mine or through a booby trap, I don't recall which. They also -- once they got more used to us and we had a longer conversation in the evening about the conduct of the entire Vukovar operation, they then expressed their anger with the manner in which this whole operation had been carried out by the command of the JNA and by the Defence Ministry. We were then told that they themselves had gone to -- back to Belgrade to complain about how the war was being run and specifically how the whole attack on the town of Vukovar had been run. In a later conversation with three or four of these men after the fall of Vukovar during an evening that we had together in Belgrade, they again mentioned this, and that they were still angry. These were not men particular -- who at the end of Vukovar were proud of what had happened. They didn't see this as some great victory and they were also aware that the whole of Vukovar had been completely destroyed during this operation. And they themselves said that this should have been unnecessary, that a professional army should have been able to take a relatively small baroque on the Danube in a matter of days rather than taking two months and destroying it completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did they tell you during this conversation if there was a specific person that they saw in order to complain, in order to try to have changes?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They told us that they had gone to General Kadijevic who was at the time the federal Minister of Defence of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you get any feedback if there were actually any changes into this effect?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They told us that there had been some small changes but that no major changes had been made. We had heard rumours in Belgrade that certain professional officers in the army had gone to Kadijevic to come, but this was the first time that we heard it actually corroborated that this had taken place. We did not hear that any major changes were made, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You said here that Vukovar -- that they themselves mentioned that Vukovar was completely destroyed. I would like to you ask you because you were out in this field, this area that we saw on the map before, as a professional war correspondent, and as you also had been saying told us that you have a great deal of experience to covering different wars. Can you tell us and for the Court how you would describe the destruction yourself in terms of your own experience, destruction of Vukovar in the -- and also in the neighbouring areas compared to other areas in the former Yugoslavia and externally?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, during the Yugoslav war - certainly in Bosnia - one encountered villages that were completely destroyed and where all the houses had been burned specifically in eastern Bosnia the only town that was totally and utterly destroyed that I saw was the town of Vukovar. When on the 19th of November, we were first able to walk the streets of Vukovar in relatively -- relative safety, when the shooting had stopped, one of the things we did to get a real view of the entire town was go to the water tower and climb up the water tower and then look over the entire town. And what we saw and what we filmed was the destruction practically of every single house. No building was unscathed. Most buildings had lost their roofs. It was a town that was totally destroyed. When we went there to the water tower, we went there with the captain and with the Lieutenant. They came up the tower with us, and they also said "What have we taken? We have taken rubble."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yeah, that could be Your Honour, yeah. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have the first afternoon break now and resume at 10 minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, when you spent time with the specific guard unit that you were talking about earlier and you had possibilities and have talked with the soldiers, did at any time the soldiers talk to you about the purposes of the attacks?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, they did. But there was clearly not one point of view. As there was not, I think, within the whole of Yugoslavia. I think there was a good deal of confusion at that time as to precisely what was happening. If one spoke to various officers of the Yugoslav army one would also get different versions. Many of those who were professional officers in the Yugoslav army really saw the army as being Yugoslavia and their function, and their whole function in life was to preserve Yugoslavia. And therefore they felt that they had to take action against anyone who was threatening the preservation of the Yugoslav federal state. There were others who believed that, given the actions of the Slovene and Croatian governments, because move of the officers within the JNA are Serbs, they believed that their function was to preserve the Serb areas within Croatia for Serbia, to in a sense create a Greater Serbia. So there were different visions as to what was happening. Then there were those who believed that really their sole function was at that time to see to it that the JNA barracks within Croatia that had been surrounded by Croat forces, that the sieges were lifted and that the soldiers and officers inside were allowed to safely come out of those barracks. So one had different versions as to what was happening. Amongst the lower ranks, there was even more confusion. Again, there were some who believed that it was then the task for any Serb to stand up and fight to see to it that the Serb minority in Croatia was brought within Serbia proper and there were others who were confused completely. Indeed, in September 1991 I had an interview with General Kadijevic, the federal Defence Minister, in which I asked him about desertions from the army and he admitted to me that this was a serious problem and the soldiers who were deserting were deserting because they did not see why they were being put into harm's way, why they had to fight. We also met within Belgrade many young Serbs who refused to be called up and who went into hiding or tried to go abroad. So I think there was confusion. The soldiers of the guards unit that we spoke to, I think many were confused as well. Some felt that it was their task as Serbs to fight for a Greater Serbia but most did not. The Lieutenant was not a Serb but as I recall a Bosnian Muslim. He was a Yugoslav. But he himself was confused as to the aims that -- of the war that he was fighting in.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Were there any specific reasons mentioned during your talks with the soldiers in the guards unit concerning the siege of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I think most felt that, because there was a significant Serb minority within Eastern Slavonia, that this region of Croatia should be wrested from Croatian control but not all agreed about this. And earlier, in speaking to various JNA officers, they said the reason for the attack was to, quote unquote, "liberate" the JNA barracks in Vukovar. But that was done in October 1991 and that could not have then have been a reason for continuing the battle until the middle of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You said that the JNA barracks were - in Vukovar - liberated in October 1991. By what means do you have knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated to an earlier question of yours, we were actually taken to those barracks in an armoured personnel carrier of the JNA. So we saw it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Referring back to the time between the 12th and the 13th November when you spent time with the guard unit, could you make any observations or conclusions, observations mostly, concerning the discipline of that unit that you did spend time with?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was in my estimation, also in comparison to other units that I had seen, a professional, well-trained army unit with a clear line of command, professional in how they dealt with their weaponry, careful in how they dealt with their weaponry, and careful in how they went about their operations. They told us when we first met them on the 12th of November that they would go on an operation to take one Croat stronghold, as I recall it a house that dominated a crossroads. We asked them whether we could accompany them and the Lieutenant said no because we would get in the way. We would be a danger to his men apart from the danger we would face. As having been an officer myself, having also been trained for that kind of operation, it is the answer I would have given if I had been in his shoes. I understand his -- from his perspective we would have got in the way. As a journalist, of course, I have to ask for permission to be able to film. No, they were a professional army unit, more disciplined and better trained than other army units that we had encountered. In fact, that I ever encountered on the Serb side either during the war in 1991 or afterwards in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned here that there was a clear line of command and control. Can you expand that, explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What I mean is that within the platoon, the platoon sergeants followed the orders of the platoon Lieutenant. The platoon Lieutenant followed the orders of his company commander, and his company commander seemed to follow the orders of those above him. There was a clear line of command and people did what they were told. There was no discussion. An order was an order and the orders were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you experience this?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, we saw people being ordered to do things and then they -- for instance to take up various positions and than they went. We were not, as I said, always able to follow this attack that took place on the 13th of November of this Croat strong hold. We were taken to one part of the unit. This was a 60-millimetre mortarist who had set up fairly close to the target, I mean I can't -- it's a rough judgement, 70, 80 metres away. And typical use of a 60-millimetre mortar. He knew what he was doing. It was concentrated mortar fire, and other units had taken up other positions. They had been ordered to do so and they did so in the way of a well-trained military force.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: During those two days on the 12th and 13th November, what did you observe other -- not in terms of how the composition of the unit were and the soldiers, what they were talking about, which places did you see, what -- what could you observe?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, we were close to the centre of Vukovar so we were in a built-up area. The fighting was from house to house, to street to street. Crossing any street had to be done at speed. There was a lot of small arms fire taking place. Every single building had been hit, most buildings had lost their roofs, had the beams sticking out, and in some places holes had been made inside the building so that you could get from one house to the other without having to venture on to the streets. Classic street-to-street fighting, inner city street fighting. The one strange aspect for me which I had not encountered before was that during the night, music was played by, I don't know, not by the unit I was with, but by certain -- by units of either the JNA or of the Serb militias within Vukovar, and I was told that this music was typical Serb music played to taunt the Croat defenders within the town. This for me was something quite different, different than I had ever witnessed before in a war zone, and within the spooky atmosphere of a night in a town where shooting is going on, flares are going off, to have this music was almost like a scene from the film Apocalypse Now. It was very strange and very spooky indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: In those 24 hours between the 12th and 13th November, did you encounter any Croat defenders at that time, in Vukovar city?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I did not. The only Croats I saw were civilians who appeared on the morning of the 13th of November precisely in the area we were. These were only women, a group of about 10 or 12 women. They were led through the fighting soldiers to the rear where we were told they would be safe but where we imagined they would be questioned by the soldiers. But we did not get further access to them but -- armed resistors or any Croat men, we did not encounter during those days, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: During those days, were there any shelling going around in the city?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was shelling but by that stage, because only a relatively small part of Vukovar was still in Croat hands, I do not recall any heavy artillery being used. But there was certainly mortar fire, heavy machine-gun fire, and explosions that I expect that they -- the soldiers were carrying a weapon which we in the west call a law, it's a light antitank weapon. It's about -- it's just under a metre long, you pull it out, you can fire it once. It has a small antitank rocket in it. The Yugoslavs had their own version of this. I was aware of this because we had had this in the Dutch marine corps, and the soldiers were carrying these and these were clearly used not against tanks which the Croats didn't have but against any strongholds and you could hear those weapons being used.
