I didn't actually see one being fired but you could hear them being fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned earlier here during your testimony the use of multiple rocket launcher. Did you see kind of use of that kind of weaponry during those two days on the 12th or 13th of November or otherwise when you were in and around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We had certainly seen them being used before the 12th and 13th. We had filmed them being used. These are, as far as I'm aware, 128-millimetre multiple-rocket launchers. We had seen them being used on various occasions but I do not recall either seeing or hearing them being used on the 12th and 13th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: If I understood you right you thought or heard it before the 12th or 13th November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: During October, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: In what area?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: South of Vukovar, around the village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. When you observed as I guess the shelling at the time both prior to those two days, 12th and 13th November, and also during those two days, 12th and 13th November, can you tell us anything about the proportionality of the use of force in the area done by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Proportionality? Well, as I have said before to the Court, I did not at any time see fire from the other side of heavy weaponry on to the JNA lines. Nor did I ever hear from any JNA officer or soldier that the Croats had artillery so this was very much one-way traffic, if you wish, of heavy artillery being used systematically against Vukovar, all the way through the war, but my impression was, and our impression was, and what we were actually told by the unit that we were with on the 12th and 13th of November, was that the battle was practically over. It was the last remnant that was still holding on and that the town was about to fall completely into the hands of the JNA. But certainly before that, we had repeatedly seen different artillery units deployed as typical artillery batteries firing at Vukovar and firing sustained artillery fire, sustained multiple rocket launcher fire and it was all going in one direction. It wasn't as if they were being fired on themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Next occasion when you and your team entered Vukovar, when was that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Why didn't you go to that area of Vukovar between the 12th November and the 18th November?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Between the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Between the 13th, I'm sorry, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We tried. We were given permission by the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade, but we were stopped on the roads and we did not manage to reach into Vukovar as we had done on the 12th, on any of the other days. Until the 18th, when we didn't actually enter Vukovar but, I think we were stopped in Negoslavci. We were told there that there were negotiations going to take place for the surrender. There we again encountered Mr. Sljivancanin and a delegate from the International Committee of the Red Cross, and we then were told to follow to the negotiations and those negotiations led to the surrender of at least part of the Croat fighters and the civilians within Vukovar which we then filmed. It was really only on the 19th of November that we entered the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Take one step, step by step, thank you. So on the 13th -- you were trying to get access if I understood you right, between the 13th and the 18th November and first on the 18th of November you had possibilities to have access to Vukovar. Were you?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: -- ever stopped in that period of time between the 13th and 18th of November? Were you then given a reason for why you couldn't enter the city?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you ask for it?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Absolutely. And we in fact -- we argued quite strongly. The field producer and myself without actually talking about it developed a good cop-bad cop routine whereby he would try because he spoke Serbo-Croat to speak pleasantly and I would now and again lose my temper if we were not given access and he would then try to explain that if I didn't get access and didn't get a story that day, that my job would be under threat. That worked on some occasions. It did not always work. And on those days we simply encountered checkpoints who said that we were not allowed through, that they had been given orders not to allow us through without any further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And then on the 19 you got access to Vukovar. Was it also the same procedure that as you told before, that you left Belgrade early in the morning? And what route did you then take on the 18 when you are entering Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. On the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: On the 18th?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Sorry, on the 18th, the road, again we had got permission from the Ministry of Defence the nights before. We drove to Sid to get the second permission. And then we took the roads from Sid through Tovarnik, Oriolik, to Negoslavci, and as I recall, in Negoslavci we were stopped and told that these negotiations for the surrender of at least part of the Croat force and of part of the Croat civilians still in the town was then taking place and that we should go to those negotiations and we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Where was those negotiations taking place? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We drove in a convoy with JNA vehicles, a number of JNA vehicles, and the vehicles of the International Committee of the Red Cross, for a while, I can't recall precisely how long, a route that we had not taken before and finally stopped at what appeared to be a deserted farm house, as I recall a small white house. To that house a delegation of, I think, three Croats was brought on foot and negotiations then took place. As I recall, I was not personally allowed into the house, but my cameraman was, to film the beginning of those negotiations and, after that, the cameraman was told to leave and we waited outside --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: -- until those negotiations had been concluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When you were waiting outside, what happened next? You were standing there outside and waiting and what happened next? What did you observe? Did you meet any specific person or what happened?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There were various officers of the JNA there and there was the ICRC delegate there. As I recall, the three Croats who had come to negotiate were brought back into town, obviously to talk to their people, and we were told that the negotiations had been successful, the ICRC delegate, as I recall, told us that, and that a surrender would take place that afternoon and we were then taken to another place where the surrender took place. And this was a road, as I recall, fairly close to the Danube, and at a certain moment during the afternoon, quite late in the afternoon, as far as the sun is concerned, but this is November so I can't remember the precise time, we then saw the people who came down the road. The army had deployed various armoured personnel carriers, and a quite large number of soldiers alongside the road, beside the road, not on it, and they had also set up one point where those who laid down their arms would be frisked. We were allowed to film all this and then both the men who -- the soldiers or the Croat fighters and the civilians who walked out of the town, we were told that it was about 4.000 civilians and several hundred fighters. They were led further on to buses and driven on. We asked whether we could go to where they were taken and permission was denied, nor were we told to where these buses were headed. And once surrender had taken place, we again took the normal -- we were driven back and then drove to Belgrade to edit our story and send it to our office in London.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Just go back a bit here. You mentioned that you were waiting outside, as you said, as a white building a small white house and you saw also ICRC there as well, and also you said here that you saw JNA officers. Are there any -- is there any man that you can recognise that were present there as a JNA officer of at this point of time?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There was a -- I think he was a Colonel. I cannot precisely remember his name. I think it was something like Pavlovic but I'm not certain of this. A man who we were to encounter again. Mr. Sljivancanin we had met in Negoslavci, talking to the ICRC delegate which is the first moment that we met the ICRC delegate and were made aware of his presence in the area and that there were going to be surrender negotiations that day, something that we hadn't known before we left Belgrade. But I do not remember Mr. Sljivancanin being present at the actual negotiations. He may have been but I do not recall if he was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You mention here that Mr. Sljivancanin were present in Negoslavci. Can you tell us what happened then, when you observed, concerning Mr. Sljivancanin at that time?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He was in conversation with the ICRC delegate through an interpreter. I imagine an interpreter brought by the ICRC. I imagine that they were talking about where the negotiations for the surrender were going to take place and possibly also about who would be present. We were kept slightly apart when that conversation was taking place. But later we were able to, because we knew Mr. Sljivancanin already, and then we introduced ourselves to the ICRC delegate and explained who we were. We were not the only journalists there I should maybe mention at this point. It was not that a large crowd of journalists were there, it was a relatively small one. But as I recall, somewhat to my own dismay I have to say, it was my direct competitors from BBC television and independent television news from Britain who were there. None of the American networks were there, as far as I recall, and Serb journalists. It was a relatively small group that had been allowed to be there and who was there subsequently when the surrender took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: How many could it be about, when you said a small --

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't remember it being much more than around a dozen people.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And when were they present, this -- the BBC and INT and yourself? When were they present under what kind of -- which procedure, under which procedure were they present?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we can talk about a procedure. They, like us, had managed to get to Negoslavci. There, like us, they had heard there were going to be negotiations for a surrender and this they like us were told that we could follow in this convoy to this deserted farm house where the negotiations finally took place. And then they, like us, were told that we could go to the place where the surrender took place and that they were able to film that. So they got there separately from us to Negoslavci. After that we were all together.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: How was this surrender organised? Can you have any view of that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not precisely. I mean, I think a time must clearly have been said to the Croats that there would be a certain moment that they could cross the lines as they were doing, that they should come at this specific road, and that they should walk down the roads. I imagine that they were also told that any person coming could only take light belongings with him. We saw a number of civilians who were carrying small bags but it wasn't as if anybody was bringing a horse and cart and lots of furniture. Only things like belongings that they could carry themselves. It was clearly also, I imagine, although this wasn't told to us, that the -- throws who had been fighters in the Croat amongst the Croats, should bring their personal weaponry with them. As I said earlier, these are only light weapons that they brought, Kalashnikovs, pistols, revolvers, and ammunition. At a certain point they were told that there they had to lie down and literally lay down their arms on the ground, this is what they did, and they were then frisked and taken along with the civilians to the waiting buses. Clearly a time had been worked out, a road had been said where this surrender should takes place, but for the rest, if anything else, was discussed between during the negotiations I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When you observed the men laying down their weapons were those men in uniform or was it a mixture, can you tell us anything about how they were dressed, the men who would lay down their weapons at the surrender place?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was immediately noticeable to us that not one of the Croats was wearing uniform. They were all in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you see what happened with the -- you mentioned here about 4.000 civilians. Did you see anything what happened to those civilians?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Civilians walked as the soldiers did -- I mean, the Croat fighters did, all down the same road. They came together. It wasn't as if there were separate groups. It was a mix group. There were men, women, and children of various ages. There was no taunting from any of the soldiers there, which was something of a surprise to us. Many were crying and many were clearly fearful. But they were led to buses and taken away. That's what we saw, and as I said earlier, while we did request permission to film them on the buses and to see where they were being taken here, for -- this permission was denied.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what happened then you went back to Belgrade, I assume, after that, as you told us earlier that that was your normal procedure so to say in order to report. What happened next day? When did you leave Belgrade next day on the 19th November?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As usual we left in the early morning at around 4.30. And drove to Sid and then took the same road from Sid through Tovarnik, Oriolik, Negoslavci. There were checkpoints. We were let through. And we drove on into Vukovar and we had -- we were told there that the fighting had stopped. We found once again the same guards unit that we had been with before, and the lieutenant with whom we had been before then dispatched some of his men to go with us around the town. Most of this we did on foot. At some moments we also drove in our own cars but we were then told that it was relatively safe to walk around but that we had to be with military because there were a lot of mines and booby traps and therefore it was considered safer for us by the lieutenant for some of his men to accompany us.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Vukovar that day?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise time but we stayed there it throughout the morning and into the afternoon. I imagine that we left at around 4.00 in the afternoon but I don't have a precise time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You said that you found the guard unit that you have encountered earlier, earlier occasions when you arrived into Vukovar. Where did you go? You said that you were also allowed to walk around quite freely. Where did you go in the Vukovar city and what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were taken by, as I recall, two soldiers, right into the heart of the town. There, we witnessed a large mass of civilians for the second day in succession coming out from where they had been hiding clearly and being led by soldiers of the JNA from the centre to the outskirts. And we filmed -- we filmed that. We encountered an incongruous scene in the centre of town where early in the morning a group of people had described themselves as being with Mr. Seselj and some who described themselves as being Chetniks, Serb -- extreme Serb nationalists were already drinking. They had even set up a music installation and were partying amidst the ruins of the town. We walked through various streets there, big and small. We saw that there were people -- still corpses lying on the ground, some people who had clearly died some time before but we also saw in the city centre a number of people who had been killed very recently. There were soldiers shooting at various points in the air, I should say, but it was clear that some of these soldiers had drunk quite a lot of alcohol and we were careful in our behaviour. But one of our reasons for being there was that we were aware of the fears that some kind of massacre might take place once Vukovar fell and one of the things that you do as a war correspondent is that you try as best you can by being a witness there to stop such things from taking place. I remember a discussion with Martin Bell, the correspondent from the BBC, about precisely this matter and an agreement that we wouldn't film in the same places, that we would move around separately as much as possible, and I know of at least one occasion, I remember at least one occasion that we warned the men that we were with that we saw a Croat male being taken away by some of Seselj's people and they then intervened and saw to it that this man was further taken away by JNA soldiers rather than by these militiamen. We ended up at the hospital, Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Excuse me, do you remember the time about when you ended up at Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It would be in the afternoon but a precise time, no, I don't. I imagine we got there 2 or 2.30, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And why did you end up at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, if -- in fact, you can see it on the map here, if one has gone through the centre of Vukovar and one is going on foot --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to interrupt the witness now. Which map is that that you're looking at? Is it the --

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't know what number it would have for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The earlier map that --

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, it's a more detailed map --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Detailed map?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: -- which shows the JNA barracks the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The Nova Ulica and the Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. So that is Exhibit number 59. Yeah, okay. We have that. I refer back to my former question: Why did you end up at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, if one takes this map, I think there is a pen that I can --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: -- maybe use but I'm not sure where it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The usher will help you there.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Sorry. We had entered along the road from Negoslavci. I cannot remember precisely where we parked our cars but we would then have walked. We were taken to the water tower, this still by the platoon commander. And then later on we walked through the town and we ended up at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Before going into the hospital, you mentioned here the water tower. Were you up in the water tower?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we were. We went there both with the platoon commander and with a company commander and both of them came up into the water tower, which itself had been very badly hit themselves, and there we could see the whole of Vukovar and Borovo Naselje below us.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And how did it look like? What did you see when you were standing up there in the water tower and looking on Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There was a major fire in Borovo and what we saw below us was a town that had been completely destroyed. House after house had been hit. Roofs that had gone, only the beams that were left. A city that had practically been completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Then you ended up at Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And once again, what time do you think it was when you ended up at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I think somewhere in the afternoon. It was certainly the last thing we filmed that day. One reason for remembering that is that I had to do my piece to camera, that is to say where a correspondent talks directly to the camera, otherwise known as a stand-up-er, and I did that at the hospital and it's the last thing that we did before going back, returning to our cars and then returning to Belgrade to edit and file our piece. So it was certainly in the afternoon but a precise time, I can't -- I can't give you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And before continuing here I would like to have the marking of the map done by the witness tendered as evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 135, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When you went to the hospital, what did you then observed regarding the hospital itself, the building or the buildings?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The hospital had clearly suffered severe damage. A number of direct hits, from a variety of weaponry and here we are talking heavy calibres but I cannot say precisely what calibre shells had hit it but it had certainly been very severely hit. All floors showed damage. It was clearly that -- in a very poor state indeed. And when we were inside, we were told that all the upper floors had been evacuated and that all the wounded were congregated in the basement and that's where we found it and it was packed with wounded. We were told that there were several hundred people in there and it was certainly packed with people, men, women, and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You said here that you entered the hospital and you were inside the hospital in the afternoon of the 19th of November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the hospital, inside the hospital, and making observations?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I suspect we stayed there around an hour but I cannot recall precisely how long we stayed there. We tried to find and we did find one doctor who spoke English. We interviewed her, both about -- she was from -- originally from, born and bred from Vukovar. She told us about the town and she had a family, and about her feelings of now having to leave this town. She was aware that she was going to have to leave and possibly never to return. She also told us of the medical conditions, the fact that they lacked water, electricity, medicine, plasma, told us of the fact that within these confines, these very, very full basements, there had been absolutely no privacy. I remember her telling us that women had had to give birth in full rooms or in corridors and that a number of babies had been born there, amidst the devastation. I imagine we were there for about an hour. She was the one person that we were able to interview. We asked to speak to the director of the hospital but -- who -- I think it was a woman, but we were not able to meet her, and then as I said we went outside. I did my piece to camera and then we had to leave in order to get back to Belgrade to file a report to London.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When were you in the hospital and you said here that you were mostly in the basement, were you able to move around in the basement when you were in the hospital, in the afternoon of the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, we were able to move around in the basement, in the corridors, in the various rooms, but I cannot say that I went into every single room in the basement or every single corridor, no. We went into a number of rooms, into a number of corridors, but I cannot recall if I -- no, I don't think I would have gone into every single room. It was -- it was quite a big building. But we certainly tried to see as much and film as much as we could down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you during the -- when you were observing, when you were in, inside the hospital, did you recognise or see any weaponry around, any weapons around in the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, we did not. We clearly saw some people who had been wounded, who it seemed to us it was probable that they had been Croat fighters but we did not see any weaponry, nor did we see any uniformed men.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Were there -- what kind of feelings did you yourself had when you were inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What kind of feelings does any human being have when they come into a place where the smell is horrific and where the agony of many was clearly horrific as well? Even with those who were not physically wounded, you could see that there were very deep mental scars because of the experience that they had gone through. One felt enormous pity for the people that we saw. It was not a pleasant experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You mention here there was a smell. What kind of smell was that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, all hospitals have a certain smell of antiseptic. Here it was not so much antiseptic but of a hospital that was not -- had not been able to be properly cleaned, where there was a lack of antiseptic. You smelt death, that sweet smell of death, and the smells of excrement, of -- that it was not a clean place. It was a pretty foul smell.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you hear anything of -- any kind of evacuation mentioned during the time when you were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In talking to the doctor, she made the clear point that the wounded in this hospital were not being -- because the hospital simply couldn't, were not being given proper treatment, and that evacuation of the wounded was an absolute necessity as quickly as it could be possibly arranged. And we imagined that this would be a high priority. When we left, as I recall, we encountered the ICRC delegate outside the hospital, and as I recall again talking to Mr. Sljivancanin, and while they were not willing to talk to us at any length, the ICRC delegate, as I recall, did indeed confirm that he was there to organise the evacuation of those in the hospital and that clearly had to be a priority given the terrible state that many of those wounded were in.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You mentioned here that the ICRC was outside the hospital and was it correct of me to understood it that also Mr. Sljivancanin was there at the same time?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's as I recall it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Were you present at the time?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, I mean we encountered them as we left, as we came out of the hospital, before leaving, that we met them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you hear any kind what they were talking about, if they were talking to each other and what --

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The only thing that the ICRC delegate told us was that he was negotiating the evacuation of the wounded, and that's all we heard and we left them to it because we had to get back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Did you go back to Vukovar after the 19th November?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes we did. We went back on the 20th of November, the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And when did you start in the morning? Was it the same route as you have described earlier from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It's the same routine. The early morning routine of leaving Belgrade at 4 or 4.30 in the morning, driving to Sid and then from Sid through Tovarnik, Oriolik, Negoslavci, into the town. The only difference on this occasion was that we headed by car all the way through Vukovar to the hospital because we were aware that by that stage, all the civilians that were -- have been evacuated or at least taken to the edge of town, but the story then for us the story in news terms was what was going to happen at the hospital as far as the evacuation of the wounded within the hospital was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you go directly to the hospital in the morning when you entered Vukovar or did you pass any other area so to say before you came to the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, we would have driven through the town, and you needn't have to have to have driven through the town centre to get to the hospital. Whether we stopped on the way to check again with the guards unit that we had been with before and with whom we had been the previous day as well, that I can't remember. We may have done. It may well have been that we first stopped with the guards unit before driving on. I certainly remember seeing the lieutenant from the guards unit that we had been with previously at the hospital and it is quite possible that he came with us. What I remember is that for him it was the first time that he was at the hospital that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I do understand that it's difficult with time and it's quite a long time since this happened so to say but can you say an approximate time when you arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: At sometime in the morning. It was certainly in the morning but I cannot give you a precise time now, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Is it possible to give you an in between time? How long did it take normally to go by from Belgrade to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Give a precise time, as to when we ended up at the hospital is, after all these years, very difficult. I mean I would -- it was in the morning certainly. I remember then waiting outside the hospital for quite sometime. I imagine we were there at maybe nine or ten in the morning but I do not have a precise time myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. So you arriving at the hospital. What did you observe at the moment when you arriving at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, firstly that there were JNA troops there, and that we were not allowed to enter into the hospital proper. We were allowed on to the compound, on to the grounds of the hospital but we were not allowed into the basement of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Who said that, that you were not allowed to enter into the hospital itself? You were there the day before.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The day before, there had not been soldiers on the doors. Now there were. And we were not allowed to enter. The soldiers told us. What we did find was where the smell of death came from and we found this walled-in small compound where a lot of the dead soldiers and civilians were lying outside, unburied, not in coffins, clearly they had been put there by the hospital staff who had not had the time or the possibilities given the conditions of the siege to bury these dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You mentioned here that you saw JNA troops when you arrived at the hospital. And when you are saying JNA troops can you describe the amount of soldiers, military vehicles? Can you paint a picture for us in this term?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not in great detail. There were soldiers. This is normal in a war zone so nothing to greatly surprise us that they were there. It didn't also surprise us because it was clear that in any evacuation, that the soldiers would play a part, the JNA would play a part in organising the transport of the wounded and the staff of the hospital from Vukovar. I don't remember any great concentration, I don't remember tanks, for instance, or anything of that nature. So it was just, I don't know, I cannot give you a precise number but there were soldiers there and it was the soldiers who, and this I do remember, that we were not given access, we couldn't go inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you try to get access into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we wanted to enter. But we were told that we could not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you talk to anyone specific about that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: To the soldiers there, who were there. I don't remember any immediately at the beginning talking to anyone specifically. Later on, we did talk to Mr. Sljivancanin about this because we encountered him, and, but again, I don't have a precise recollection of the time frame that this happened but that he was there again with the ICRC delegate. There was an argument going on between them which we filmed from a distance, and then we spoke to both of them, and when we spoke to them about the reasons for their argument, the ICRC delegate did something which ICRC delegates usually don't do, and that is to make a statement in front of the cameras. The International Committee of the Red Cross has a policy basically of not talking to journalists and this was unusual for him to do so. The only thing he told us was that his work and that of the ICRC had been made completely impossible by the JNA. Off the record, i.e., not in front of the cameras, he told us that they had broken the agreement that they had earlier agreed to between the JNA and the ICRC and that they had entered the hospital. That's the only thing he told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And when was that? You said they entered the hospital. Did you say --

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, he said that they had -- sorry for the translation. He had said that -- he said to us then that they had entered the previous evening, the 19th of November. We also spoke to Mr. Sljivancanin about the reasons for his argument with the ICRC delegate and he told us that the ICRC delegate was naive and that he didn't seem to realise that this was a war zone with a war going on, and, as I recall, he also accused the ICRC of not being impartial in the conflict but that is all that we were told at that time and I do not recall being given an explanation as to why access inside the hospital was denied to us on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: This discussion or argument between Mr. Sljivancanin and the ICRC representative, where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The one that we filmed was right in front -- I mean, at the doors. Just outside the hospital, at the doors of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And when you're saying at the doors of the hospital, do you today remember which side of the hospital or which kind of building it was because we know that there are different, the hospital contains of different kinds of buildings?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is at the main building of the hospital and I imagine at the main door but I cannot remember on what side it is. I saw the hospital on two days of my life, on the 19th and 20th of November. It was certainly the main big building. I imagine at the main door. But more precise, I cannot be.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you or did your team approach the ICRC representative in course of this argument?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not while the argument was taking place. When they had stopped arguing, they really came, as I recall it, the ICRC delegate came to us and then said, "I want to make an a statement." And as I have explained to the Court, this is very unusual in my own experience of dealing with the ICRC in various parts of the world, in Yugoslavia, in the Middle East, and elsewhere. I am not used to the ICRC wanting to make on-camera statements. But he was clearly very angry and wanted to protest via us to the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And Mr. Sljivancanin, did he -- did you approach him or did he approach you, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't know whether he came to us or whether we came to them but we clearly wanted to speak to him to get his view of what was happening and why there was a row. It was not clear to us at all at that stage why there should be a row between the JNA and the ICRC, so whether he came to us or we went to him, I -- I don't recall but he clearly had his response that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And did you -- at this time did you observe were there any people around in the compound or was it empty? Can you explain for us what you saw around in this -- in the compound of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were a number of ambulances there, ambulances of the JNA. Precisely what time the buses arrived, I cannot recall, but I don't think that they were there when we arrived. But there were a number of military vehicles and there were a number of ambulances. I recall a number of military green ambulances, different to civilian ambulances that had clearly already come there to take away the more heavily wounded. I remember one older, wounded person was loaded into one of these ambulances and, as I think, with -- it was I think it was a woman, with her grandson, a boy of eight or nine years of age, something of that nature. But the -- most of the people including the doctor that we had interviewed the day before, we did not see until they were loaded on to the buses, as I recall during that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You mentioned here people loaded on to the buses. Did you see that and where? And what -- and how many buses was it?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. We did see, and film, the people coming out of the hospital. The walking wounded, civilians, men, women and children, and the medical staff, walking from the hospital on to the buses that were parked on the hospital or by the hospital grounds. I can't give you a precise number of buses. As I recall, four or five buses. There were a number of military vehicles there. There were ambulances as well and at a certain moment the buses left. We followed them, we filmed them for part of their way. But not the complete way. At a certain moment we were stopped because we were told that these buses were driving basically towards the front line and were then going to cross the front line into Croatian-held territory and therefore that it would no longer be safe for us to follow them. Later, however, that did not succeed and we encountered them again, this time with three -- now the ICRC was no longer there as I recall but the ECM were, this is European Community monitors who were known as the ice cream salesmen for their white clothes. They had blue arm bands with the 12 gold stars on it of the European Union. And there again we encountered the officer, the JNA officer, whom we had also seen at the farm house during the negotiations on the 18th. I think as I said earlier I think he was called Pavlovic but I may be wrong there. And there we were told that the buses had tried to drive into Croatia proper but that they had come under fire from the Croatian side and therefore had to turn back. And then we finally we were told that these buses were going to be driven to Sremska Mitrovica and that the non-wounded would be put up at I think a sports hall there and the wounded would be taken to hospitals in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to the hospital. And when you observed people were loaded on to the buses. Can you describe what kind of people it was, gender, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I think I've already mentioned, men, women and children of various ages. Some of them were wounded, some of them were not. Many again were in tears, just as we had seen on the 18th of November. The buses were full and some of them were overcrowded with people having to stand, but men, women and children, so -- of varying ages, old and young.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Were you able to talk to any one of those people?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I remember, we didn't. And so I imagine that we were stopped. But I'm not sure about why at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: M'hm. Did you see any other kind of buses than those buses that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: These were civilian buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you see any other buses than those civilian buses?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, no. The only other vehicles in this convoy were ambulances that I mentioned earlier and there were some military vehicles, I imagine, as -- as -- at the front and the back of this convoy. But the buses were of a military -- of a civilian nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Once again I do understand that it's difficult with time but I do have to ask. You mentioned, described here how you left the hospital area and followed after the buses. Can you remember approximately what time it could have been when you left the hospital area?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid I find it very difficult, so many years on, to give you a precise time. I imagine in the early afternoon but I cannot be certain. We did film the buses later on. It was still light when we filmed them later on when they were heading for Sremska Mitrovica so I imagine it was at the beginning of the afternoon. But I cannot give you a precise time, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Can you estimate how long time you were at the hospital compound area in the area that were you standing and waiting, et cetera, before you left the area of the hospital? One hour, two hours, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I would estimate that we were there for several hours. I remember hanging around. It's part of life for any correspondent in a war zone, that you hurry up and wait, and that's what happens with the military, if you're working with the military. And it's something that we get accustomed to, that we are told to hurry up and get somewhere and then that we sit around and wait. And there was some hanging about and waiting there yes, certainly, but I cannot give you a precise time. Several hours, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Van Lynden. There are two videos that will be asked by the Prosecution to be tendered into evidence and that I would like to show the witness. And also the Judges, of course, and the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are these very long, Mrs. Tuma?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: No. But we can take it after the break. The first video is about six minutes and the next video clip is about two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, we'll see those now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I also would like the witness to make comments concerning the -- regarding those videos.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: In -- the first video, is from the 65 ter list, it's number 341 and it bears the ERN number B0004593 and that is an extract over a longer video and it starts with -- from the beginning and the extract will end at 000638 about. And I will ask the witness to look at this video and the rest of us, of course. And then afterwards, I will ask the witness to give comments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest that it had better then be replayed and start from the beginning if you want comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, it must be from the beginning, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: "The last of a hundred thousand shells, a hundred thousand [unintelligible] millions of bullets. For the Croats on Monday, the three month old battle of Vukovar is lost but not quite over. Die-hard Croat guards holding out even as hundreds of their comrades and thousands of civilians surrender to the federal army. A long, weary column shuffling out of their own town forever. Many are in tears. Many are in shock, or simply in despair. A scene of defeat which silences the victors looking on. Perhaps because of the quiet nobility with which the Croat fighters lay down their arms. Only for a few is the humiliation too great to bear. But most eyes retain a defiant pride in having held out for so long. The following day, the battle over, more neighbours emerge out of the ruins of Vukovar's town centre. They have survived and leave. Dragging their only possessions after them, the slow march to a new existence, the bleak one of refugee. Like almost every other structure the town's main hospital has been maimed, probably beyond repair, and yet it hadn't closed, the confines of its basement offering sanctuary to over 500 wounded. Here they had coped with no electricity, no water, few medicines. Here there had been no privacy but over 30 births, and here they tried to save even the smallest of lives. "She is six months old and she is very badly wounded here in her leg. And she has one little part of the shrapnel of the bomb in her stomach and she needs really -- how to say it?" "Better hospital?" "An operation, operation to save her life. We are doing our best but I think without transport, her in somebody's centre and better conditions, it is so she will die, I think." "Around the hospital there is an all encompassing stench of death and the soldiers soon discover why. An open morgue of those hospital staff did not have time to bury. And with its fall Vukovar reveals the dark secrets of its war, its roads, the dead who never reached the hospital, or who, the blood still fresh, were clearly murdered. "If the ruins of Vukovar symbolise anything at all it must be the hatred that still exists between the Serbs and Croats that lay dormant during 45 years of peace that has now expressed itself in a mutual commitment to war, a commitment which does not appear to have been satisfied even after three months of fighting here. "And amongst the horror, there is the surreal incongruity of celebration, extremist Serb militiamen, and women, posing triumphantly for an end-of-battle photograph before returning to a morning feast of music and laughter fueled by alcohol. "The motto on their flag is freedom or death and they vow they will fight on. "No it's not finished "What for you do the Serbs need to take before the war is over?" "War will be over when we have our limits, Karlobag, Karlovac Ogulin, Virovitica. All places where Serbian people live must be free, you know. We must clean up with the Croatians "In the town centre other militiamen display an uncontrolled rejoicing and a similar frame of mind. But the army's engineers are certainly not celebrating. Instead, clearing unexploded ordnance. Or searching for the anti-personnel mines and booby traps the defenders left behind. To find them is a delicate task, to clear them less so. "And it takes another day before the wounded of Vukovar can be evacuated, a painful, chaotic exercise. It takes hours before the ambulances have been loaded up. The walking wounded reached the overcrowded buses and dusk is approaching when the convoy finally departs taking its occupants on a last sight-seeing tour of destruction before leaving behind a once beautiful town on the River Danube, rendered silent by the victors and the vanquished, lost to its inhabitants, an obliterated memorial to hate."

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Van Lynden, do you -- what's happening here? Do you recognise this video?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: By what means, then?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is a compilation that I made after the end of the battle of Vukovar, so a day on the 21st or on the 22nd of November. I can't remember the precise date. Usually, the pieces for the news would be shorter than that. This is a much longer piece. And it was an overview of the last days of the battle for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Would you please comment on this video, what we can see on it?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The first shots on the video are not those taken by a Sky News cameraman and these were pictures taken, I believe, by Reuters television, of the last fighting in the town, and the pictures after that are all taken by Sky News cameramen apart from, I think, there is one shot or two shots in there of a number of dead bodies in the centre of Vukovar. Again those pictures came from Reuters television. The rest is all ours and what they show us is what happened on the 18th, 19th, 20th, as far as we were able to record it. So the last shooting in the town, then the surrender on the 18th, then the other civilians in the city centre coming out of their shelters on the 19th, and finally the evacuation of the hospital on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Also there was a sequence of celebrations so to say, at least I saw men drinking?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. These were I think I've referred already in my earlier testimony to the Court about this. These were people who described themselves either as Chetniks or as militiamen of Mr. Seselj, and who were on the morning of the 19th of November we found them in the city centre. They had set up music there, they had alcohol with them, and they were celebrating which, given where they were, and given their surroundings, we found incongruous, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And I recall a man on this video having a ribbon around his forehead and, if I remember it right now, he said, "Clean up the Croats."

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you encounter this man?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. He was in this group of celebrating Serb militiamen - these were not members of the JNA - and he was the one who spoke some English and so you in fact actually hear me asking the question on the tape as to how long I ask him this war has to continue? And he then says that the war has to continue until the Serbs have reached their limits, I think is what he calls it and he names four towns in Croatia. I was later told by my field producer that he had not named the towns in the right order, which was a signal to my producer that this man didn't really even know what he was talking about, but what he was saying was that they had to do all the way wherever Serbs lived, that these areas had to be freed. And this was certainly what the other militia men were saying but this was the only one who was speaking English and so this is the only one with whom I could have a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Is there any other comments you would like to say concerning this video?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, the only thing I just noticed is that I hear myself saying that it's only at dusk on the 20th that the buss could leave from the hospital so in answer to your earlier questions that must have been the case. But as I wrote that on the 21st or 22nd of November 1991, that's -- obviously I remembered then rather more clearly than I do now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move over to the next video clip. And that is not in our 65 ter list. It bears the ERN number V0006475 and it's a short extract. This video has been disclosed to the Defence last week.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: "They are pawns in a game of ethnic politics. The Croat wounded of Vukovar are awaiting to be evacuated from the town's devastated hospital and handed over to the Croatian authorities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber has no view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: "But even as the walking wounded slowly made their way --"

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Take it from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could we play it again from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: "But even as the walking wounded slowly made their way towards the waiting buses, politics intervened. First between the delegates of the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Yugoslav army, the JNA, the ICRC accusing the army on having reneged on two agreements. For instance, allowing its soldiers into the hospital compound. It's not their usual way but on this occasion the ICRC made its wrath all too plain. "The International Committee of the Red Cross is completely unable to perform the task that was entrusted to it by the parties. "For their part senior army officers responded by accusing the ICRC of bias and of a naive lack of understanding that Vukovar was in a war zone. A war zone with a hospital at its heart. The area reeks of death and the soldiers soon discover why. "Precise casualty figures are not available but hundreds fell and tens still lie --"

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden could you please comment on this on this -- regarding there video?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is the story, the report that I did on what happened on 20th of November 1991 from Vukovar. The -- which led to the eventual evacuation of the wounded and the civilians from the hospital complex out of Vukovar. And it shows also the argument between the ICRC delegate and Mr. Sljivancanin taking place at the entrance to the hospital and it shows the statement that I had said the ICRC delegate had made, very unusual for an ICRC delegate to make, a statement of this nature, and then the riposte from Mr. Sljivancanin as we had filmed it. That's basically what this tape shows.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like to tender both videos into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, I'm asked about the transcripts of the videos. Are you wanting those tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All -- then each video and separately and each corresponding transcript will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 136 for video number 1, Exhibit number 137 for the transcripts of video number 1, Exhibit number 138 for video number 2, and Exhibit number 139 for the transcript of video 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mrs. Tuma, that clearly is an appropriate time for the second break. We will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I'm done in examination-in-chief by this. So it's perfectly good timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As Mrs. Tuma has now finished her questioning, it is time now for Defence counsel, if they have questions. Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, I could not see Mr. Domazet who was hidden behind the pillar. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Van Lynden, I am Vladomir Domazet and I represent Mr. Mrksic. Good evening. I'm going to be asking questions as co-Defence counsel for Mr. Mrksic. First of all, Mr. Van Lynden, several questions about your extensive CV. If my understanding is correct, you started working as a journalist as early as 25 years of age, all over the world, in fact. Would that seem to be a fair assessment? Would I be right in claiming that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also said that you served in the Dutch military in a variety of units, that you became a reserve officer, and that the whole training took about two and a half years. This is probably before you started working as a journalist. This roughly speaking would be your professional background, isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Before I went into the military, I completed a Bachelor of Arts degree in sociology and politics at Durham University in the United Kingdom. I didn't serve in a variety of units. I served only in the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps. The training period was one year for a reserve officer. After that I served as a second lieutenant, as a platoon commander, and as a commander of a mortar platoon. And yes, that was prior to becoming a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another question in relation to your present career. You mentioned that you now teach at the American university in Bulgaria. My only question would be which is the subject you teach there?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm the chair of the department of journalism and mass communication and I teach journalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go back and dwell on sometime on Vukovar. Although in your capacity as a correspondent you've been to most parts of the former Yugoslavia, most of those affected by war anyway, I will dwell on Vukovar alone. What I want to know is whether you had prior knowledge of Vukovar before you reached Vukovar in your capacity as a correspondent. Above all, I wish to know whether you were aware of the ethnic makeup of the town before the war.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. I had not been to Vukovar before the war. I had been to Yugoslavia before the war but not to Vukovar, and I was only told about the ethnic breakdown of Vukovar once I came to Belgrade in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991, before the events in November that you described, did you go to Vukovar in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It would be fair to say that the first time you arrived in Vukovar was in November, then, if I'm not mistaken, it's the period between the 12th and the 20th of November, with several days' break when you did not travel from Belgrade to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. The first time I remember entering Vukovar was, as I've already stated in my testimony, when I was put into an armoured personnel carrier and driven to the JNA barracks in Vukovar, and, as I recall, that was in October 1991. I did go to the outskirts, I mean to Negoslavci, places of that nature, between the 13th and the 18th but we were then stopped from going into the city proper, not by staying in Belgrade but by not being let through the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During your visit, did you find out or were you told what had been going on prior to your first arrival there? More specifically, the relations between the Croats and the Serbs in Vukovar and its surroundings? As you know, it was a multi-ethnic town.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I had been told that it was indeed a town with a mixed population, and I was aware and had been told that there had been fighting in or problems in various parts in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you find out how it was that the first clashes broke out in Vukovar prior to the period that we are now discussing and before you ever arrived there? Specifically, did you hear anything about barricades being erected separating individual neighbourhoods or villages in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I cannot recall getting any precise information as to what had happened in Vukovar itself, but I had heard of other barricades or roads being blocked off in other places, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned that you first went to the barracks which at the time was not blocked. Did you at any point in time hear that the JNA barracks had been laid siege to?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. That is what we had been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke about those who were fighting in Vukovar, one of my colleague's friends [as interpreted] was whether those surrendering their weapons were wearing uniforms. As far as I recollect, you said they were not. Do you have any idea at all what sort of uniform they could have been wearing? Did Croatia have a regular army with proper uniforms at the time?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Sorry, are you saying that the people who surrendered on the 18th of November were wearing uniforms? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, no. That's not what I'm saying. But this is precisely my question: Do you know if Croatia had an army of its own at the time? I'm talking about November 1991.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Firstly, I had seen dead Croat fighters with a uniform of sorts, not as I recall around Vukovar, but in other parts of Croatia. And as far as I'm aware, Croatia did not have a proper standing army when the conflict broke out, after their declaration of independence in June 1991, but they then started forming one as happened in Bosnia a year later. And there were units that were uniformed, but I suspect it was a mix of uniforms as well. But I didn't operate on the Croatian side during the war. I operated on the Serb side, and those were the people that I was observing directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that there were units in Croatia wearing all sorts of uniforms, but what I'm really interested in is what you observed in Vukovar. My next question is in relation to your first visits. You mentioned that at the outset, you had been working with a cameraman who was local, a Serb, I assume, who travelled with you from Belgrade. That being the case, do you remember this person's name by any chance?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, he did not travel with us from Belgrade. He was already there with a reporter from Belgrade television. And we simply linked up with him and were able to get a copy of the pictures that he took and to be able to do a piece to camera. This was right at the beginning in Banija, in 1991, and only at that stage. I don't recall the name either of the cameraman or of the reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that in order to reach the area, there were two paths. One was through Sid and Tovarnik and the other through Erdut. If travelling through Erdut, that means approaching the area from the north. Would I be right in saying that you would not have been able to reach Vukovar or, rather, the southern sector of town where the military units also were? What about the roads in the northern area, Erdut, and the ones in the more southerly area that you passed on the way, as you said?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, there were basically two fronts, the northern front and the southern front. If I wanted to go to the units of the JNA on the northern front I would have to cross the bridge at Erdut. If I wanted to reach the units on the southern front, I would have to go through Sid and Tovarnik. On the whole, we did it on the southern route but on several occasions we did it on the northern route as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were at the northern front line, in order to reach the southern one you would have needed to return to Serbia and travel for quite a while in order to reach the other area. Wouldn't that seem to be the case?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Certainly at the beginning. As far as I could observe what was happening is basically an operation, a pincer operation, to make it a noose around Vukovar. One operation from the north, the other from the south and on the eastern side Vukovar had, of course, the River Danube, and, indeed, certainly at the times that I recall going in October, on the northern front I would not have been able to drive apart from at enormous personal risk to go from the northern one directly to the southern front and I would have had to go all the way round.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Today, you testified about damage in such places as Tovarnik and Ilaca. In Ilaca you saw a house in flames. In Tovarnik you saw damage to both churches. What I would like to know is if you can provide a little more detail. Where were these towns at the time? Which country did these towns belong to? Based on the information you had at the time, what was the predominant population of those towns? I'm referring obviously to their ethnic breakdown.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Tovarnik was in Croatia, which depending on your point of view was either an independent country or one of the republics within the Yugoslav federation. So was Ilaca. I do not -- they were not towns, they were villages, and I do not know their precise ethnic breakdown. What I am aware of was that in Tovarnik there was both a Catholic, Roman Catholic church and a Serb Orthodox Church, therefore giving me the impression that this was a mixed village. One other point. I did not see one house burning in Ilaca but several.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I did say "houses." It may have been a misinterpretation. We do have an understanding on that issue. When you spoke about this, you mentioned something you referred to as the official border between Croatia and Serbia. At the time, there was no such thing as an official border separating the two countries. I would like to hear an explanation on what precisely you had in mind when you used this term.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, there is a precise border. There was even when Croatia was a part of the Yugoslav federation. There was a precise demarcation line. That's -- I'm not referring to customs or passports controls because they did not exist, indeed, but there was a precise line of a borders of all the republics that made up the Yugoslav federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is certainly the case. There were borders, no doubt. However, up to that point, there had been no official border crossings. There was nothing to show that you were actually crossing a republican border, that is until the war. That is what my question was about. You spoke about tanks and said that to your knowledge only the JNA had tanks. Did you ever see at the northern front line or at the southern front line any of those tanks destroyed?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do not recall seeing any tanks of the JNA destroyed, no. If we had, we would have filmed them. I have absolutely no recollection of ever doing so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Talking about Vukovar, did you perhaps ever hear that prior to the time when you first arrived, right at the very outset, one or two military planes belonging to the JNA had been shot down over Vukovar by the Croatian forces? Is this something that you heard?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I cannot remember hearing that, no. I may have done but I cannot remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: About your travels from Belgrade to Vukovar and the other way around, you said today that you needed to obtain a permit in Belgrade but that despite this sometimes you were not allowed into the Vukovar area. Can you perhaps remember who was it specifically that denied you access on particular occasions and did you ever have an opportunity to bring this up with superior levels of the army, if the army was the body in question?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was at army checkpoints that we were stopped, and without them giving us precise reasons told that we could not go further. I remember one occasion that, and this would have been in September or early October -- no, September, definitely in September, that we managed then to get access to a general whose name I'm afraid I don't remember precisely, something beginning with an "A," Aligevacir. I don't know the precise name. And he then saw to it that we were allowed to enter as far as Ilaca. On another occasion when we had seen the general again, and this is a story that I told in my earlier testimony to the Court, about a convoy that was to go into Vukovar that day with medical supplies and to take out the wounded, that the general had told me that the convoy would take place and that we were stopped in Negoslavci and that a lower officer of the JNA told us that the convoy would not take place and that we could not go any further on that day. If we were stopped on other days, it was generally at checkpoints and generally not by officers but by possibly a sergeant in the army and we were simply told that we could not go any further despite the fact that we had been given a permission, both at the Ministry of Defence and at the forward office of the Ministry of Defence in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you encounter the same problem with the members of the guards unit that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. We -- the members of the guards unit that we were sent to, we were sent to only after we met Mr. Sljivancanin and he said that we could go to them and he arranged that we went there and we were then taken to this platoon commander, a lieutenant, and that was -- that was the case on the 12th of November. But we only encountered it -- him inside Vukovar. As I recall, at the JNA barracks or somewhere at that -- on the southern edge of Vukovar, not on the road beforehand, at Oriolik or Negoslavci. And those were the places where we were usually stopped and not allowed to go further, and specifically Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned today the fact that you talked a number of times with members of that unit, with some officers, that sometimes you spent an entire night with them and you spoke about the unit. What I want to know is what you learned at the time or any observations that you may have had about that unit. You talked about a professional relationship. I'm not going into further into that but do you perhaps know that this was a unit it would had many more officers in its ranks than ordinary soldiers, as it were, and that this was a special anti-terrorist unit by nature?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was immediately clear to me that I was dealing with professional and well-trained soldiers. Their uniforms and their equipment was different. They had for instance bullet-proof jackets, that either units certainly did not have. They had different helmets. Also for communication. I cannot be -- recall that they told us that they were an anti-terrorist unit, no. The Dutch marine corps also serves as the anti-terrorist unit within the Dutch armed forces. Therefore, I have some experience as far as that is concerned. They were a professional unit, better equipped and better armed and clearly better trained than other units that I encountered, but I can't recall that they told me that they were an anti-terrorist unit. As far as your question related to officers and men is concerned, I met a platoon lieutenant and his platoon was not populated with other officers but with lower ranks. I cannot say whether it was -- that we met all 30 men of what would have been a standard platoon size but I certainly met a number of men who were serving the lieutenant and they were of lower rank, either non-commissioned officers or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you were following that unit through the town, also in the situation when they were going from house to house or street to street, at least that was what we were able to see on the footage we received from the Prosecution, and even you yourself ran across the street with them, if I'm not wrong about what I saw on the footage, and then went with them to their next position. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: If I can just first clarify that we were only with this unit during the actual fighting on the 12th and 13th of November. Those are the only two days we were with them during the actual fighting of -- in the battle of Vukovar. We encountered them again on the 19th and on the 20th by which time the fighting had ended. To say that we followed them, we went where they took us and where they allowed us to go and as I think I've already explained in my testimony, the orders for the lieutenant were to take a certain house, as I recall a Croat strong point on a cross roads, and he would not let us come on that operation directly. We were allowed to film and he took us to where a mortarist with a 60-millimetre mortar was shooting at that or firing mortar bombs at that position but he didn't take us with him when he actually attacked that strong point for the reasons that are also I have already given and which I personally understand, that he felt that a television crew would endanger his men and the operation and that it was too dangerous for him therefore to allow us to come along. But we did cross a number of streets, when they took us. It depended on them, not on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During the time that you spent with that unit, you said which period that was, did you notice anything in the conduct of the soldiers or the officers that would deviate from regular conduct during war operations or anything that would deviate from rules of war?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not get an impression that their conduct was anything other than as professional soldiers. What for me I observed is that they were quite different to the other units of the JNA that I had encountered and the various militias, specifically Mr. Seselj's people, that had also been allowed into the front lines of Vukovar by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. When you talked about weapons, especially the weapons of those who were in Vukovar and who were surrendering their weapons because you were present at that time, you said that they were mostly light weapons. Later, did you and your crew find weapons that were discarded? I'm specifically talking about Zoljas or some anti-aircraft weapons that were perhaps abandoned in town by throws who were using them. Do you recall anything like that, in view of the fact that there is footage of that. Of course, I'm not sure whether that's your footage although we did get that footage as being the footage of Sky News.

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Okay. If I may first just clear up footage of Sky News, there is footage directly taken by Sky News cameramen and there is footage that will have been broadcast by Sky News that has come to them from other sources. One major source of footage during 1991 was Belgrade Television. The other one was Reuters TV. I do not personally recall ever filming any heavy Croat armaments in Vukovar.
