The soldiers that we saw surrendering -- or the soldiers that Croatian forces that we saw surrendering on the 18th of November only had Kalashnikovs and handguns. I didn't see any other kind of weaponry being surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did they perhaps take you personally to any of the bases that remained after the fall of Vukovar? Did they take you maybe to some stronghold or some storehouse? Do you recall anything like that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What I recall for the 19th of November is that when we had made contact with the platoon with whom we had spent the night on the 12th, 13th of November, that they took us, they had found an underground tunnels that they showed us that they said had been used by those defending Vukovar. No arms were there. There was bread waiting to be baked and there were dishes that had been washed up and they showed us that. They -- we also saw engineering units, as I think you saw in the piece that was broadcast earlier by the Prosecution, of the engineers blowing up ammunition that had been left behind. And we were taken to these minefields that had been planted and that besides the roads and that were got rid of in a, for me, novel manner, of the soldiers simply shooting at the mines and blowing them up. But we were never taken on the 19th to a base, what had been a Croatian army or forces whatever you want to call them, base, during Vukovar. Possibly, because they had not yet been discovered or at least not with the knowing that the unit that we were with was not aware of them. And so we were not taken there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. When you talked about arriving at the hospital the first time, you said that that was sometime in the early afternoon. You said we arrived at the hospital. What I would like to know is who did you mean when you say, "We arrived"? Who came with you and entered the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Throughout those days, when I say "we," I'm referring to the four-man team, that is myself, the field producer, the cameraman and a sound recordist, so four people from Sky News.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said today that you were looking for and that you did manage to find a doctor who spoke English and you took her statement or you interviewed her. Is that the lady we saw in the footage, the doctor speaking, or is that somebody else?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. That's the doctor speaking on the footage that you were shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned that -- you mentioned that you knew that the director of the hospital was a woman and you mentioned that you didn't see her. Do you know why you were not able to see her?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I didn't know beforehand that the director of the hospital was a woman. We were told inside the hospital, as I recall, and no, I do not recall why we could not see her but we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: While you were going around seeing the patients in the rooms, you went not everywhere, of course, but were you accompanied by any soldier or were you thwarted in any way as you were touring the hospital and as you were going to see whatever it was that you wanted to see in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, when we arrived at the hospital, there were no soldiers, and when you mentioned soldiers, I imagine you mean soldiers of the JNA. I do not recall seeing any soldiers of the JNA there when we arrived, nor do I recall seeing any soldiers of the JNA inside the hospital while we were there, nor do I recall seeing any Croat in any kind of uniform while we were there. No, we went in, we weren't really led around. We filmed. Nobody stopped us filming. We asked to meet the director of the hospital, as I've already mentioned. And we found the one lady doctor who spoke English. The field producer talked to other people but we did not as far as I recall do any further interviews. When we left the hospital, it is my recollection that then for the first time, I did see a JNA soldier and that this was Mr. Sljivancanin and that this was -- and that the ICRC delegate whom we had met the day before was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you talked about the convoy's departure from the hospital the following day, you said that you had information that it was going in the direction of Croatia and that it had been turned back and that later it went to Sremska Mitrovica. Do you remember that that was what you also told the cameraman in one shot as the buses were passing by you, as you were saying that?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did. I think it was a closing piece to camera with the buses coming by me, saying that they -- that the Croats of Vukovar were going to end up in Sremska Mitrovica, indeed, yes. Where we indeed also found them the next day because on the 21st of November, that's where we went to Sremska Mitrovica to see what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So the footage related to this second attempt by the convoy to leave Vukovar, when you already knew that they were going to Sremska Mitrovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When I was speaking in front of the camera with the buses going behind me, yes, the buses were heading for Sremska Mitrovica, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you said that, and I think it was today also on the footage, you said that over 500 wounded were at the hospital. Do you remember perhaps where you got this piece of information from? Do you remember who told you this information?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I don't. I imagine that I must have got that information from the doctor that we spoke to inside the hospital, but I don't remember precisely at this moment who we got that information from, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, you said a little bit earlier when I was asking you about the convoy, that the next day you went to Sremska Mitrovica and you saw that those people had gone there. I hear that it was not recorded in the transcript exactly in that way so I'm asking you again. The following day you went to Sremska Mitrovica to make sure that the convoy had actually gone there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: On the 21st, I remember going to -- I think it was a sports hall in Sremska Mitrovica and finding that the people who were evacuated from the hospital, who were not wounded, had been taken there. We stayed there until they were again loaded on to buses and this time driven from Sremska Mitrovica into Bosnia. And that's the last we saw of them. After they went into Bosnia they were able to enter Croatian territory. We had also asked to find other busloads that -- for instance, of those that surrendered on the 18th but that was -- permission was denied and we were not told where they had gone to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm talking about the convoy that you saw off and that you then followed. So you know that this convoy did reach Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, but the only thing being that those who had been wounded were taken off and I imagine were taken to hospital but I don't know where. But I imagine also in Sremska Mitrovica but we don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, do you remember in your statement, and let me ask you first, of course, you remember giving statements to the investigators before your testimony here today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I remember giving statements to the investigators, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you recall saying at the time that what you saw, from what you saw, the JNA was protecting both the civilians and those who were surrendering their weapons from the paramilitary units that were in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is indeed what I said and what I saw in Vukovar. I saw -- on the morning of the 13th of November, I saw civilians, a small group of civilians, coming past the mortarist from the guards unit we were with and they were led by soldiers to the rear; that I said in my statement and that is what I said in my report at the time. On the 19th, when we were in the centre of town and a large group of civilians were leaving the town, again I saw soldiers of the JNA accompanying them out of the centre of Vukovar to the outskirts of the town, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. When we were talking about this convoy earlier that returned from its attempt to reach Croatia, did you find out how the convoy was prevented from getting to Croatia? Did somebody stop it, or was it fired upon?

utterances.speaker: AERNAUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We didn't ourselves see why it was stopped. We were told by JNA officers that it had been fired upon by Croat forces, and this was off the record, so not in front of the camera. This was confirmed to us by the monitors from the European Community, and that is what I reported leading to a number of direct statements and attacks from the Croatian government on me personally for making that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. Mrs. Tapuskovic, is it practical, do you think, for you to commence now? There seem to be four minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would suggest that we finish for today because I am unable to complete the cross-examination of this witness in four minutes. We only have four minutes left and that is not enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That seems a practical position, Mrs. Tapuskovic. As indicated, we've reached the end of our sitting day, short now of three and a half minutes. We resume tomorrow in the afternoon, at 2.15. And we would be grateful if you were back here to continue. We are progressing well with your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will be here tomorrow afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will adjourn now to resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
